title: Terminology and notation
text: An Alabama county and a California school are both units, but their reports compare different outcomes. The definitions below specify what is compared, how the posterior enters the comparison, and which reports can be chosen.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Targets and posterior uncertainty


Unit; criterion k

A unit is a firm, school, site, or other entity included in the comparison. A criterion is an outcome or other target used to evaluate the report. For example, income and incarceration are two criteria measured for the same counties.
Examples: Multiple criteria · Supplied summaries

θᵢ

The target for unit i, coded so that higher values receive higher reporting priority. The application states what higher priority means for that target.
Examples: Two-unit comparison · Alabama counties

Posterior

The distribution of target values given the data and model. Posterior risk averages the loss over this distribution. Calibration concerns how those probabilities agree with outcomes under a specified evaluation law or in new data.
Examples: Posterior shrinkage · Posterior inputs

πᵢⱼ

The posterior probability of a direction such as Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ). This calculation uses the joint distribution of the two targets because the event depends on their difference.
Examples: Direction probabilities · Interval overlap

eᵢⱼ⁽ᵏ⁾

The probability that stating i above j is wrong on criterion k. Under the zero-margin weak-error convention, equality makes either strict direction wrong. If equality has positive probability, the two directional errors sum to more than one. Each example specifies the event and any comparison margin.
Examples: Pairwise decisions · Posterior equality

Marginal interval

An interval containing a specified share of the posterior distribution for one target. A 90% interval for each of two schools gives a probability statement about each school individually. The probability that one school’s target exceeds the other’s uses their joint posterior.
Example: Report-card summaries

Expected rank

The posterior average position of a unit under a specified rank and tie convention. Ordering these averages gives one possible ranking and can define a fixed-order report family.
Example: Alternative ranking summaries

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Grade reports, disclosure and error


Common-grade report g (P1)

An ordered grouping of the units, with grade 1 at the high-priority end. The report states a direction between grades. Within a grade it leaves the comparison unstated. Using the report to allocate places or resources requires a separate rule.
Examples: Report construction · Allocation objectives

n, M

The number of included units and their M = n(n − 1)/2 unordered pairs. Each cross-grade pair contributes one stated direction.
Example: Report-family counts

N, s = N/M

The number of stated pairs and the disclosure share. The remaining M − N pairs are withheld.
Example: Disclosure from tier sizes

Eₖ

The posterior expected number of wrong stated directions on criterion k, obtained by summing directional error probabilities over the stated pairs. Joint correctness is a separate probability.
Example: Expected and realized errors

Eₖ/N

The expected wrong share among stated pairs of a fixed report. It is NA: no disclosure when N = 0.
Example: Error-rate denominators

DRₖ = Eₖ/M

The expected wrong count per possible pair. Withholding can reduce this rate by reducing the set of stated directions. The criterion subscript is usually omitted in single-criterion examples.
Example: Error-rate denominators

τ

The cost per withheld pair when a wrong stated direction costs one. Weighted risk is R_τ = (E_w + τ(M − N))/M.
Example: Reporting risk

λ, ϕ

KRW’s reward for a correct direction and the informed share in their stipulated audience model. The conversion is τ = λ/(1 + λ) and ϕ = 1 − 2τ. The positive-cost audience range is 0 < λ ≤ 1, 0 < τ ≤ 1/2 and 0 ≤ ϕ < 1. Equivalence of optimal reports requires the stated common-posterior, tie-free and common-family conditions.
Examples: Loss-scale conversion · Equivalent reporting losses



A loss-minimizing report satisfies E_w ≤ τN when the family includes the report that withholds every comparison. The inequality follows by comparing the chosen report’s loss with that benchmark. A grade report chosen by a different rule may exceed the benchmark.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Report families and comparisons


Family; grade cap

The set of reports considered in the search. A grade cap limits the number of grades. A fixed order limits grade boundaries to cuts along that order, so the best report among those cuts may differ from the best report over all orders. Some fixed orders also keep equal scores together.
Examples: Report families · Computation methods

Frontier

The lower convex boundary of expected wrong counts plotted against disclosure for a specified report family. A point on an edge may require randomizing between complete reports. Two reports can minimize risk at the same τ while stating different numbers of pairs.
Examples: Error–disclosure frontier · Comparison constraints

ψ

The probability of choosing the report that states more pairs in a mixture of two frontier reports. Expected disclosure averages the two pair counts using the mixing probabilities. An individual draw produces one of the two complete reports.
Example: Mixtures of reports

wₖ, E_w = ∑ₖ wₖEₖ

Nonnegative criterion error weights summing to one, and the weighted expected wrong count. These weights apply to directional losses. Coefficients of a scalar composite target have a separate role.
Examples: Common grades · Composite targets

qₖ

An expected-error budget, expressed in count form as Eₖ ≤ qₖN. With no stated directions both sides are zero, although the error share is undefined. Some applications use budgets only to evaluate the displayed report; others use them to restrict selection.
Examples: Budget-constrained families · Case-report checks

Δₖ

The risk of the common report on criterion k minus the minimum risk for that criterion under the same loss and report family. If the exact minimum is unknown, bounds on it give an interval for the excess risk. Changing the loss or family changes the benchmark.
Example: Criterion-specific excess risk

Selection belief; evaluation law

The distribution used to select a report and the distribution used to evaluate that fixed report. Using a different evaluation law can change expected loss for the same grade vector.
Examples: Alternative evaluation laws · Selection-draw evaluation

Joint correctness

The probability that all stated directions are correct together. Pairwise probabilities and expected wrong counts alone do not determine this event probability. Composite targets similarly require the relevant joint-law information.
Example: Limits of pairwise probabilities

Simulation error

Numerical uncertainty due to a finite set of posterior draws. Independent draws and dependent chains require different variance calculations and diagnostics. Increasing the number of draws reduces numerical error under the supplied law without establishing the adequacy of the model.
Examples: Independent-draw error · Dependent-draw error



When repeated reports state different numbers of pairs, averaging their realized error fractions gives equal weight to reports that state at least one pair. Dividing expected wrong counts by expected stated counts gives more weight to reports that state more pairs. A posterior-reported share instead uses the probabilities supplied to that report. Averaging across reports compares these quantities, and the case-report tool specifies the denominator used in its report.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Domain profiles and joint protection
Domain profiles give each unit a grade for each domain. The following definitions explain how those grades are compared and how joint errors enter the choice of a report.


Domain d; profile matrix G

A substantive reporting coordinate and its grade column. The matrix has units on rows and domains on columns. A common-grade report uses the same column across criteria; a multidomain profile (P2) permits separate columns. Grade 1 denotes the highest reported priority within its own domain.
Example: Common grades and domain profiles

Profile tuple; crossed directions

A unit’s ordered domain grades. Tuples such as (1,2) and (2,1) place the first unit higher in one domain and lower in the other. They do not define an overall ranking or an allocation rule. Equal grades within a domain withhold that pair’s direction without asserting equal latent targets.
Examples: Common and profile reports · Forty fictional sites

Complete joint state

A set of target values for every included unit and domain in one posterior state. A complete finite law lists each possible state and its probability. Two laws can agree within each domain and differ in how the domains vary together. Row labels on separate simulations are insufficient to recover that dependence.
Example: Dependence and joint protection

F_d, N_d, R(G)

In a joint state, F_d counts false strict directions in domain d; a strict assertion at latent equality is false. The reported card discloses N_d pairs in that domain. Its additive expected loss is R(G) = ∑_d w_d{E(F_d) + τ_d(M − N_d)}/M, with the original M = n(n − 1)/2 pair count. This expected cost is distinct from a probability that one or more protected conditions fail.
Examples: Separate weighted choices · Reporting resolution

t_d, α, J(G)

A strict false-direction-proportion threshold, an inclusive joint cap, and the direct union probability J(G) = Pr{at least one d: F_d > t_dN_d}. The union is formed within the same joint state before its probability is calculated. At N_d = 0 the ratio is not defined and the domain’s exceedance event is false. Feasibility requires J(G) ≤ α, alongside any other declared constraints.
Example: Dependence and joint protection

Separable reporting decision

An additive weighted objective whose actual feasible family factors into a Cartesian product of domain choices. Every combination of the complete weighted domain minimizer sets is then optimal in that product. Posterior independence is unnecessary. A zero-weight domain contributes every feasible column to its weighted minimizer set, while retaining its constraints. A joint constraint can prevent the feasible family from factoring.
Example: When domain choices separate

Occupied-grade counts (K_S, K_C)

The numbers of occupied grades in the two domains, rather than a particular site’s profile tuple. With a fixed law, loss and candidate bank, relaxing a budget cannot increase minimum risk. A selected domain’s grade count can nevertheless decrease as reporting detail moves to another domain. Count paths identify the canonical representative when there are tied optima.
Example: Posterior uncertainty and reporting resolution

Exact optimizer set; displayed representative

All feasible candidates that attain the same exact minimum loss. The app displays the first in a specified grade order and keeps the other tied reports available. The reported optimum is relative to the candidates included in the search.
Examples: Common versus separate columns · Dependence and tied cards

Exact calculations for a finite law

For a complete list of posterior states and probabilities, the app computes losses and tests constraints with exact fractions. A separate assessment is required if the supplied law approximates another posterior. The browser examples accept 2–4 units, 1–2 domains, 1–8 states, and at most 256 distinct profile cards, with at most 256 input columns per domain. The R package also supports assessment with independent draws and MCMC diagnostics.
Examples: Joint-law illustration · Specified reversal scenarios

Saved profiles for fictional sites

The forty-site example shows grade tuples, the settings used to choose them, and separate summaries for selection and diagnostics. The grade tuples identify occupied cells and the directions stated in each domain. Rerunning selection or computing new risk probabilities would require the original joint draws. The stored fractions describe the draws used. The diagnostic segment came from the same chain as the selection segment, so it does not provide an independent validation.
Example: Profiles of forty fictional sites

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text: Three summaries of the same posterior can give different rankings. The figure compares the posterior mean, the expected rank, and the posterior probability of belonging to a specified top group. Expected rank averages a unit’s position over the posterior, with rank 1 assigned to the largest value. The first example uses three units to show why these summaries can order a pair differently. The simulated league shows how much uncertainty remains in a unit’s rank and how a change of measurement scale can alter an ordering by posterior mean.

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three-unit law, posterior mean. A has the largest posterior mean, a value it takes in neither state, yet its expected rank, 2.4, is the worst: A is first with probability .3 and last otherwise. The two orders differ on 2 of the 3 pairs.
Three-unit law, first place. B is the most likely to be first (.7); C never is.
Three-unit law, √θ. On the square-root scale A’s posterior mean falls to 1.34, below B’s 2.00 and C’s 1.73, so the first column now follows the expected ranks: 0 of the 3 pairs differ.
League, expected rank. U13, a small unit with posterior SD .120, is 6th by posterior mean but 8th by expected rank (9.59): the large units U06 and U24 pass it. Its 90% rank interval runs from rank 1 to rank 24. The two orders differ on 6 of the 435 pairs.
League, top ten. U21 is the unit most often in the top ten in 4,000 Monte Carlo draws (.96; one standard error is below .01), ahead of U26 (.94), which has the largest posterior mean. Two units are never in the top ten.
League, exp(10θ). On this scale U13 climbs from 6th to 3rd by posterior mean (4.09), and the posterior-mean order disagrees with the expected-rank order for 40 of the 435 pairs.







We specify the three-unit distribution and the league’s posterior directly. postrank uses these distributions as inputs. Rankings by posterior means appear in Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section IV.B and the notes to Figure 2C, where empirical Bayes posterior means are coarsened into deciles and quartiles; talk slide 59 sets such rules beside their grades for the firms. Their Section II.F names the expected rank.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text: Under a normal likelihood and a common normal prior, the posterior mean averages the estimate and the prior mean, weighting each by its precision. Those precisions are the inverse squared standard error and the inverse prior variance. The resulting mean minimizes posterior expected squared error. The figure traces the change from each estimate θ̂ᵢ in vermilion to its posterior mean in navy. Estimates with larger standard errors move farther toward the prior mean. When the standard errors differ, the order can change. A common standard error preserves the order.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text:
Numerical illustrations

Prior SD .15. Small units move .64 of the way to 0, medium units .31 and large units .10. The units move toward 0 by different amounts, reversing the estimated order for 37 of the 435 pairs in this draw.
Prior SD .05. A narrower prior increases shrinkage: small units move .94, large units .50, and in this draw 71 of the 435 pairs change order.
Every SE .10. A common SE gives a common retained share, .69, for every unit: no lines cross, and 0 of the 435 pairs change order.
Against the true values. In this draw the average squared distance to the true values (crosses) falls from .0163 to .0096 and the spread from .162 to .098, below the truth’s .149; yet 14 of 30 units end farther (ringed).
Too narrow a prior. A prior too narrow for these true values can even raise the average: at prior SD .02, .0197 against the estimates’ .0163 in this draw, and .0191 against .0175 over many draws.







Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, estimate their prior from all the firms (section III, slide 49); it is not normal, depends on each firm’s SE (section V.B) and, for race, puts all its weight on positive gaps. So State Farm’s race estimate of −.544 (SE .444) has a posterior mean of .155 (90% interval .014 to .342, from a smoothed version of KRW’s posteriors). In their data, ranks from linear (James–Stein-type) shrinkage “perform substantially worse than naively ranking the point estimates” (section V.E). The postrank theory book (ch. 20, “Empirical Bayes specification”) sets out their prior; the normal prior here is a teaching simplification. title: Expected errors in a strict ranking
text: A strict ranking makes a statement about every unordered pair. With n units, the triangular matrix contains the M = n(n − 1)/2 statements. If the ranking places i above j, the statement has posterior error probability 1 − πᵢⱼ, where πᵢⱼ is the probability that i has the larger true value. We sum these probabilities to obtain the expected number of wrong statements. Many of the most uncertain pairs contain nearby ranks. As the pairwise probability matrix shows, imprecise units can be difficult to order even when the ranking places them far apart.

title: Expected errors in a strict ranking
text:
Numerical illustrations

97 firms. Kline, Rose and Walters’ (KRW) firms, ranked by posterior mean, make 4,656 claims; the posterior expected wrong count is 1,249, more than one in four. Ranked by estimate they expect 1,395 (the two orders disagree on 639 pairs); KRW find the posterior-mean order close to their best strict ranking (Section V.E), but that is not a general rule. Here 35 claims sit above one half.
Top 10 by posterior mean. 45 claims, 18.22 expected wrong. By comparison, ranking all 5,834 California elementary-type schools with at least 30 students counted in the case study would make 17,014,861 pairwise claims.
Six sites. 15 claims, .7194 expected wrong. The highest dot, C above D, is a claim between neighbors, wrong with probability .362.
League of 30. 435 claims; 94.48 expected wrong, 102.2 by estimate (37 pairs differ). In the simulation we can compare the ranking with the known true values. The ranking makes 88 wrong claims in this draw and 80.69 on average.







KRW’s race card at λ = 1 is also a full ranking, in a slightly different order, so it expects 1,248 wrong claims where the posterior-mean order expects 1,249 (KRW’s archived reward path). The expected count is a sum of probabilities over all the claims, not a list of particular claims. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only. Changes: race pair probabilities as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw); firms ranked here by posterior mean, top-n blocks and expected counts computed in this browser. No endorsement is implied. title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text: Each cell gives the posterior probability πᵢⱼ = Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ ∣ Y) that the true value for row i exceeds that for column j. Equality has posterior probability zero here, so the transposed cell gives 1 − πᵢⱼ. Sorting by posterior mean places many of the least certain comparisons near the diagonal under independent normal posteriors. Comparisons between units with imprecise posteriors may remain uncertain even farther from the diagonal. Changing the sort moves each unit’s row and column together. The probability for a given pair stays the same.

title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, by posterior mean. C above D, .638, is the least certain direction, and its cell is next to the diagonal; A above B (.812) and E above F (.856) follow. Below the diagonal each cell is one minus its mirror: D above C is .362.
Six sites, by label. The label order already follows the posterior means. C above D still has probability .638.
League, by label. Of 435 pairs, the least certain, U19 above U25 at .502, sits 6 cells from the diagonal. None of these 10 least certain pairs is next to the diagonal; the farthest is 26 cells away.
League, by posterior mean. The middle-blue cells now form a band: U19 above U25 is next to the diagonal, and so are 8 of these 10 least certain pairs; the farthest is 2 cells away.
Two imprecise units. At prior SD .10 the cell in row U22, column U25 is 5 cells from the diagonal, yet its probability is only .528: both are small units with posterior SD .089.







The six sites are fictional after-school sites, A to F, from postrank’s tutorial data: their normal posteriors for the reading score are set by hand and taken as given. An evaluation office grades them to set the order of its visits. The league is that of Ranking noisy estimates, with the posterior of normal–normal posterior shrinkage. Two imprecise units can have direction probabilities near one half even when they are far apart in the ranking. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024) plot these probabilities for pairs of first names in Section IV.B, Figure 2A, and talk slide 38. They refer to the posteriors as beliefs. Slide 54 shows the same heat map for the firms. KRW put one half on the diagonal by convention; postrank leaves the diagonal empty.

title: Ranking noisy estimates
text: Imprecise estimates can place units near the top or bottom of a ranking even when their true values are less extreme. We rank thirty simulated units by estimate. Units with fewer observations have larger standard errors (SEs). Across samples, the true values stay fixed, letting us compare how often each size group appears at either end.

title: Ranking noisy estimates
text:
Numerical illustrations

First draw. Of the 10 extreme positions by estimate, small units hold 5, medium units 4 and large units 1 in this draw; by true value they hold 3 small, 4 medium and 3 large units.
True values. In the first draw, of the top 10 by estimate, 9 are in the true top 10 (7.45 on average over the twenty replays). U19, a small unit with true rank 11, is the first of the bottom five: Sampling error moved it down the ranking. U18, a large unit with true rank 30, sits two rows above them: noisier small and medium units fell past it, and its own estimate came out above its true value.
Twenty replays. The draw menu brings any replay into the table. On average over the 20 replays, small units hold 4.35 of the 10 extreme positions and large units 2.00, and the estimates order 83.90 of the 435 pairs the wrong way, against 88.12 expected over many draws.
Replay 11. In this replay, small units hold 2 extreme positions, medium units 5 and large units 3. Large units hold as many extreme positions in this ranking as in the ranking by true values. Their average across the replays is lower.
Extremes highlighted. When true values are hidden, the shaded rows do not identify which units have genuinely extreme values. The dashed line marks the truth, 3 small and 3 large units. Small units sit above it in most replays; large units sit on or below it.







Real units have unknown true values, so this check is not possible. The firms of Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, came with SEs of very different sizes: the race estimates have SEs from .025 to .444 (Section V.B; talk slides 47–49). title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text: A pair’s estimated error probability is the share of posterior draws in which the proposed direction is wrong. For the six tutorial sites, the figure compares these estimates with the exact probabilities. Intervals of ±2 Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs) generally narrow as draws increase. We flag a pair when its interval includes the withholding cost τ. The examples show when this sensitivity affects the coherent report.

title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

S 1,000. In this run (seed 1), A–B is estimated .198 against the exact .188, MCSE .0126 (2 MCSE ≈ .0247 with the exact e), so τ .20 makes it fragile. With at most 3 grades A and B share a grade in 100 of the 100 runs: the report changed in 0 of the 18 runs where A–B’s choice flips.
All reports. The report changed in 18 of the 18 runs where A–B’s choice flips; in 5 more runs its estimate equals τ and 2 reports share the smallest risk. The exact report is among the optima in 82 of 100.
S 100. MCSE .0402 in this run (2 MCSE ≈ .0782 with the exact e), radius .1788; the exact .188 stays.
S 4,000. Radius .0283. This run still flags A–B (estimate .203, MCSE .0064): its exact value lies .0116 from τ, inside 2 MCSE (≈ .0124 with the exact e); 54 of 100 runs flag it.
C–D at τ .35. In this run (seed 1) of 400 draws C–D (exact .362) is flagged: estimated .360, MCSE .0240. Its choice flips in 35 runs; the report changed in 0 of the 35 runs with at most 3 grades, in 35 of the 35 runs with any number.
Both scores. At seed 4, E–F’s estimate .202 lands above τ, so the report from the estimates withholds it, unlike the exact report; at seed 1, E–F is fragile at .192 yet stated.







The radius is postrank’s (postrank_iid_bounds(), no ties); the theory book’s form allows ties (4M for 2M). The envelope needs independent whole-state draws and an S fixed before drawing (an effective sample size cannot replace S in it); the MCSE shown is the IID one, as postrank_mc_fragility() computes it for independent draws (for chains it uses an MCMC MCSE). The reruns use consecutive seeds, wrapping from 4,294,967,295 back to 1 at the supported endpoint.

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text: Marginal credible intervals can overlap even when the posterior strongly favors one direction. For independent normal posteriors with the same standard deviation, the difference A − B has standard deviation √2 times the common posterior SD. The two marginal SDs sum to 2 times the common SD. The upper figure shows the intervals and where they overlap. The lower figure shows the distribution of A − B, from which we calculate the direction probability.

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Just touch, 90%. The intervals meet at 1.645, and the posterior means are 3.290 posterior SDs apart. The difference has SD 1.414. The gap in means is 2.326 of those SDs, giving A a probability of .990 of having the larger true value.
Just touch, 95%. Wider intervals touch only farther apart, at 3.920 posterior SDs, so touching 95% intervals correspond to direction probability .997.
Means 2 SDs apart. The intervals overlap by 1.290 posterior SDs, and the chance that A’s true value is larger is still .921.
Means 1 SD apart. An overlap of 2.290 posterior SDs corresponds to direction probability .760.







When two 90% intervals just touch, A is very probably the higher, .990, for two independent normal posteriors with equal SDs (.997 for 95% intervals). With unequal SDs the distance at which the intervals touch and the SD of the difference change, and the probability with them. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C and Figure 3) draw a credible interval beside each first name and use pairwise posterior probabilities to assign the grades.

Sites D and E of the package’s tutorial input have posterior means .15 and −.50 and SD .20 each, 3.250 posterior SDs apart: the app at ?gap=3.25 gives the same probability, .989, with intervals that overlap by .040 posterior SDs.

attr(m, "upper")["E", 1] - attr(m, "lower")["D", 1]   # 0.007941451 = .040 × SD .20: the 90% intervals of D and E overlap

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text: Two units can have the same marginal posterior distributions under different assumptions about how their true values move together. In a bivariate normal posterior, positive correlation reduces the variance of A − B, while negative correlation increases it. The shaded region below the equality line gives π_AB, and the ellipse encloses .90 of the joint posterior probability. The first example holds the marginal distributions and the mean difference fixed as correlation changes. The probability can move closer to or farther from one half, with the same direction remaining more probable. A second example obtains the correlation from uncertainty about a shared prior mean.

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correlation .50. The ellipse follows the equality line because the two true values move together. The difference has SD .200, compared with .283 under independence, and π_AB = .841 against .760.
Independent. Correlation 0 with equal SDs draws a circle: the difference has SD .283, and π_AB = .760.
Correlation .95. Strong positive dependence gives a difference with SD .063, and π_AB = .999.
Correlation −.95. The ellipse lies across the line, and the difference widens to SD .395: π_AB falls to .694, toward one half, not past it.
Shared prior mean. Estimates .30 and .10 with SEs .20; true values spread with SD .10 around an uncertain prior mean (SD .50). The model gives correlation .645, SD .126 for the difference and π_AB = .624; assuming independence for the same marginals gives .212 and .575. With prior-mean SD set to 0, the correlation vanishes, each posterior narrows to SD .089, and π_AB stays .624.







Where the correlation comes from. Given the prior mean, each posterior mean keeps the share k = prior SD²/(prior SD² + SE²) of its estimate, independently. Both posterior variables depend on the uncertain prior mean, so their covariance is (1 − k_A)(1 − k_B)v, with v the prior mean’s variance given both estimates (theory book, ch. 18); with equal SEs the shared part cancels from the difference. postrank takes such posteriors as joint draws, or as normal laws averaged over the prior mean (postrank_mixture_coefficients()).



Standalone: embed/correlated-units.html, for example ?corr=-.50 or ?preset=shared-mean&meanSd=0.
Related applications: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities (1.8) works the independent case; Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities (1.10) drops joint normality: there the means no longer fix the side of one half.

title: League tables and report cards
text: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), hereafter KRW, sent fictitious applications to 97 large U.S. employers. They estimated the contact advantage for distinctively white over Black names and male over female names. Ranking the estimates gives a direction for every pair of firms. KRW’s cards compare only firms in different grades. Even when both reports compare a pair, they can order it differently.

title: League tables and report cards
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race card. The table states a direction for each of the 4,656 pairs of firms. KRW’s race card states 1,324 of them (.284): 1,219 run as the table does and 105 the other way; it is silent on the other 3,332.
Second place. Nationwide is second by estimate (.402 ± .216) but shares grade 2 with 80 other firms. Of its pairs with the other 96 firms, the card states 16: 15 as the table does and 1 the other way, Genuine Parts (sixth by estimate) above it.
Last place. State Farm has the lowest race estimate, −.544, and the largest SE, .444, yet stands at rank 14 by posterior mean (.155), pulled up by KRW’s race prior (normal–normal posterior shrinkage). The card states 16 comparisons involving State Farm, 2 as the table does and 14 the other way.
By posterior mean. Genuine Parts (Napa Auto) now leads (.250), though sixth by estimate (.330 ± .071). It shares grade 1 with AutoNation, the largest estimate (.433). Now every one of the card’s 1,324 directions runs as the table does.
Gender card. The table now ranks the gender estimates. The card’s four grades, sizes 1, 3, 89, 4, state 731 pairs (.157): 730 run as the table does and 1 the other way. Builders FirstSource is alone in grade 1, so all 96 of its pairs are stated.







Sources: KRW’s Introduction and Section VI, “Racial Discrimination Report Cards” (Figure 7, the race card), Section VIII (Figure 14, the gender card), and talk slides 4–5 and 61–63 (card layout after slides 61–63). On the race card, grade 1 is KRW’s ★ (one star), which KRW call the worst grade. A shared grade means “not compared”, not “equal”. title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text: The tool builds a grade report from posterior means and standard deviations, estimates with standard errors and a prior, or pairwise probability matrices. The result names the set of reports searched. The calculation runs in your browser, where your input records stay.

title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight posterior summaries uses the first 8 units from the league example, which differ in precision. The report states 17 pairs and has weighted risk .1455.
Eight estimates, flat prior uses a normal posterior for each unit, centered on its estimate with SD equal to its SE. The grades agree with the first example even though the posterior probabilities and risk differ. Here the risk is .1368.
Eight estimates, Normal prior centers the prior at zero with SD .15. The posterior matches the first example, and the risk is .1455. The prior is a separate assumption from the estimates and their SEs.
Two probability matrices uses the supplied probabilities for two criteria at six sites. The common report states 9 pairs at weighted risk .0933. The matrices provide pair probabilities without site means or intervals.
Thirty posterior summaries exceeds the enumeration limit. The tool searches cuts of the weighted expected-rank order, which depends on the criterion weights. The best report in that order states 251 pairs at risk .1581.
All reports tied has 541 reports with the same minimum risk. The list displays the first 100 and gives the total. With every comparison withheld, the expected error share is shown as NA.

The normal-input calculation assumes that the units are independent given the model. Use joint draws or a joint law in R when the units are correlated. For matrices, specify the event and where the probabilities came from. The input assumes zero probability of latent equality and a zero comparison margin. The checks cover dimensions, ranges, and whether opposite directions sum to one. A joint law, calibration, and numerical accuracy need separate evidence. Leave unassessed units out of the input because a bottom grade would assert comparisons about them.
Apply keeps the previous report until the new input passes the checks. A download includes the input and settings used in the displayed report. The URL carries settings only, so paste the records and source descriptions again after a reload. If you open the optional joint solver, its status and gap describe the search using the supplied probabilities.
Open the standalone tool.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text:
A new set of measurements can change which units a report ranks above others, even when their true values stay fixed.
For each pair of measurements, we count comparisons that become stated, become withheld or reverse direction. We report these changes alongside the number of pairs stated and each report’s expected errors. A rule that withholds every pair is perfectly stable by this measure, but provides no directions. The simulation holds the true values and standard errors fixed and calculates a fresh posterior for each dataset under the same prior.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text:
Numerical illustrations

Optimal cuts. The first observation states 251 pairs. The second report and relation-change grid show that the criterion is the same, but the measurements and fitted posterior summaries change. The pair control selects a repeated-measurement experiment.
Estimate tiers. The first report states 300 pairs. The fixed tier sizes keep disclosure constant here, even when different units occupy those grades. The comparison table separates disclosure from the fraction of changed relations.
Prior SD .05. The same measurements are reused with a narrower assumed prior. We recalculate the posterior means, probabilities and optimal cuts under this narrower prior. The true values stay fixed.
Withhold every pair. Every relation stays withheld. The claimed error fraction reads NA: no disclosure. Its stability is no evidence that the report is informative.
τ .05. A lower price makes withholding cheaper. The histogram and disclosure column describe repeated-data stability, separately from reporting risk.







We draw independent normal measurement errors for the same units, true values and SEs. Each report’s error fraction uses the posterior from its own measurements. The pooled fraction adds the two expected wrong counts and divides by their total disclosure. The optimal-cut rule searches boundaries within the posterior-mean order for each dataset.



Standalone: stability, for example ?preset=cuts&pair=2.
Related applications: Fixed quantile tiers, Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings, Averaging error shares across reports.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text: A rule that states more pairs has more opportunities to make an error. We compare each rule’s expected wrong count with the lowest count the report family can achieve at that same level of disclosure. The boundary can include a lottery between two complete reports. The chart also marks the best single report when it can state the specified number of pairs. For rules outside the report family, the app gives the evaluated risk alone.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same N, τ .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with E 3.114. The frontier is 2.951, a gap of .1634. Open How the boundary is reached for the mixture chance .667 and the best single report at that N, with E 3.013.
Estimate tiers. Three tiers from the estimates also state 21 pairs, but their gap is .6429.
Flags. The flag report states 19 pairs and lies on the frontier: gap 0.
Strict order, τ .05. Stating all 28 pairs leaves a gap of .2305. The cross marks “risk above all-withheld” at this τ. The gap at the same disclosure stays fixed as τ changes.
At most three grades. Among 6,051 reports, the estimate tiers’ gap becomes .4796. The posterior-mean tiers reach the capped frontier, where only balanced reports with sizes three, three and two attain the endpoint.
Four tiers outside the cap. The rule is outside this family and receives no benchmark. The all-withheld rule remains available in the select, at N 0.







We evaluate all rules under the same posterior. The flags use the mean of all thirty league estimates as their reference, even when the comparison covers eight units. Each draw from a frontier lottery produces one complete report with its own disclosure count. The lottery’s error fraction divides its expected wrong count by its expected disclosure. This benchmark concerns pairwise directions under the chosen posterior and loss.









NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text: Unit A has the highest posterior mean in this three-unit example because its true value is large in the less probable state. In the more probable state, B ranks first. Requiring grades to follow the mean order can therefore exclude the lowest-risk report. The state table gives the joint posterior, and the report table shows which grades each order allows. Both orders are evaluated at the same withholding cost.

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text:
Numerical illustrations

Mean order: τ .25. At two stated pairs, the mean-order boundary expects 7/10 wrong directions against 3/10 with any order. At this price, the best mean-order cut withholds every direction at risk .2500. Searching all reports gives risk .1833 by placing B above A and C.
Expected ranks: τ .25. The order becomes B, C, A and its best cut recovers risk .1833. The highlighted summary row and report strips follow the order switch; all four rule cards remain available.
Equal risk: τ .30. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2 share the minimum. Both disclosure counts and the equal-risk tolerance are reported because the optimum is not unique.
Mean order: τ .50. The mean-order cuts have risk .4000 against .2000 for the best report. The expected-rank order still reaches the unrestricted boundary.
Mean order: τ .10. Both methods withhold every pair at risk .1000. The imposed order misses only above the cost at which disclosure first becomes worthwhile.







The result depends on the two states and their probabilities. The cut method searches every allowed boundary within one order, whereas the joint benchmark searches every report that meets the cap. A different cap changes which reports enter the comparison. Each point on the curve compares the two methods at a common cost.



Standalone: order-misses, for example ?order=rank&tau=.25.
Related applications: Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings, Restrictions on the report family.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text: A pairwise threshold reports a direction when its error probability is strictly below τ. Applied separately to each pair, this rule can produce directions that no grade report can reproduce. For example, if the report withholds A–B and B–C, A and C must share a grade too. A stated direction for A–C would contradict those two decisions. The triple display counts these contradictions and directed cycles. The card overlay shows which directions the archived grade report states under the same released probabilities.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race λ .25. Naive thresholding states 1,575 directions. Among 147,440 triples, 32,773 have two pairs withheld and the third stated. For the selected triple, the withheld pairs would force every firm into the same grade, contradicting the stated direction.
Race λ .10. The two-withheld count is 24,278. The triple selector and map arrows locate other conflicts in the matrix.
Race λ .50. The count falls to 15,107. The rule reports more directions, yet fewer triples have two withheld pairs and one stated pair.
Race λ .75. The count falls again to 3,108. Even without a strict directed cycle, the withheld pairs can conflict with a direction the rule states.
Race λ .25, card blocks. The card withholds 575 confident pairs and states 324 directions whose errors exceed τ. The selected triple retains its identity within these blocks. KRW’s card has no cap on the number of grades, so these differences arise from coherence.
Gender λ 1.00. All 4,656 pairs are stated, but 1 directed cycle precludes a coherent grade report. The absence of cycles at the race baseline does not extend to every target and threshold.







A shared grade leaves the direction between two firms unranked. We count threshold decisions using the released probabilities for the signed target. KRW selected the archived cards with their own code and archived probabilities. Here we evaluate those cards under the released probabilities and use the overlay to compare their directions with the separate pairwise decisions.
Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1, CC-BY-NC, noncommercial use only; as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw), changes noted; no endorsement is implied. Provided as is, without warranty. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.



Standalone: naive-thresholding, for example ?lambda=.25&blocks=true&triple=0.
Related applications: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions, Deciles and quartiles of posterior means.

title: Standardized-evidence flags in a league
text: The flag rule groups thirty units according to how far each estimate lies from the league mean in standard error units. It treats the reference as fixed even though the mean is itself estimated. A unit can receive a higher flag than a unit with a larger estimate if the two estimates have different precision. The matrix shows the directions implied by the flags. Once the groups are assigned, we use the posterior to count expected errors and evaluate reporting risk.

title: Standardized-evidence flags in a league
text:
Numerical illustrations

League, cutoff 1.96. The flag groups contain 6, 22 and 2 units. They state 188 of 435 pairs. Under the teaching posterior, E/N is .130 and risk is .1696. The gray row bands identify units placed below another unit whose estimate is smaller; the outlined matrix cells locate the same reversals.
Same flags, flat prior. The report still states 188 pairs. We evaluate the same directions under independent normal posteriors centered on the estimates, with SDs equal to their SEs.
League, cutoff 2.576. The stricter cutoff changes membership of the outer flag groups. The matrix changes in whole blocks: all pairs between different flag groups are stated, and all pairs within a group are withheld. A cell within a group leaves the two units unranked.
Same report, τ .10. The same 188 pairs are stated. The all-withheld comparison has risk τ = .10. The cheaper baseline depends on the withholding cost even when the report does not change.







At the first setting, 20 stated directions reverse the order of the estimates. The largest error probability is .649 even though the average error probability is below the withholding cost. That difference matters because the flag rule uses only the estimates and their SEs, with no constraint on the expected errors of individual comparisons. Both matrix axes follow decreasing estimates. Use the arrow keys or the table to read the cell values.



Standalone: flags-in-the-league, for example ?crit=1.96&prior=teaching&tau=.10.
Related applications: Grades based on standardized evidence, Posterior summaries in a grade report.

title: Grades based on standardized evidence
text: An evidence flag depends on how far an estimate is from a reference in standard error units. Here the rule uses zᵢ = (θ̂ᵢ − r)/SEᵢ with the reference r set to zero. Values above the upper cutoff receive the highest flag, and values below the lower cutoff receive the lowest. The remaining values receive the middle flag. If the flags are treated as grades, a smaller but more precise estimate can rank above a larger one. The two normal posterior specifications give different assessments of the direction these flags report.

title: Grades based on standardized evidence
text:
Numerical illustrations

Two units, flat prior. A has z = 4.00 and B has z = 1.50. The flags state A above B, although B’s estimate is larger. When each true value has a normal posterior centered on its estimate with SD equal to its SE, this direction has error probability .686 and risk .6862. The reversal comes from the difference in standard errors.
Same flags, teaching prior. The error falls to .288; the posterior means are .180 for A and .108 for B. The estimates and SEs still give the same flags. The new posterior assigns a lower probability to an error in their direction.
B’s SE .15. B reaches z = 2.00. Both units now receive the same flag, so the report states 0 pairs and has risk .2000. Because the flags match, this report leaves the pair unranked.
Cutoff 2.576. The stricter cutoff separates the flags again. The stated direction has error .736. The estimate and its SE determine the flag. The withholding cost τ enters when we evaluate the report.







NoteReading the cutoff



The cutoffs 1.645, 1.96 and 2.576 are the two-sided 10%, 5% and 1% normal critical values. A flag compares one unit with the reference. The probability that a stated direction between two units is right comes from the posterior.
This constructed comparator follows the postrank theory book, ch. 17 (the Tennessee procedure in ch. 2 uses a related index with other cutoffs).








TipIn postrank





p <- pnorm((.30-.20)/sqrt(.05^2+.20^2))
x <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(array(c(NA,1-p,p,NA),c(2,2,1),dimnames=list(c("A","B"),c("A","B"),"score")), event="directional_error", zero_ties=TRUE, margin=0, source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="Two-unit example",conditioning="Independent flat-prior normals"), targets=c(score="True value; larger is higher priority"))
postrank::postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=2L),x,weights=c(score=1),tau=.2)[c("N","E_over_N","primary_risk")]

Related applications: Standardized-evidence flags in a league, The decision for an isolated pair.

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text: A report that minimizes posterior expected loss can lose to another report in many individual states. This comparison keeps both reports fixed and evaluates them on the same posterior states. The frequency with which the comparison report has lower loss and the average difference in loss answer different questions. The finite-state example gives both quantities exactly. The simulations show how estimates of those quantities vary across samples.

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text:
Numerical illustrations

Inside the family. Among 63 reports with at most two grades, the best has conditional risk .0940; the two posterior-mean tiers have .1046. Yet that common rule wins 57 of these 100 paired draws. The difference in loss can be large even when the common rule wins more often. Points below the dashed diagonal show states where the common rule has lower loss.
Outside the family. The comparison retains the two-grade family but uses a three-tier comparator. Its conditional risk .0417 is below .0940. The search still allows only two grades, so its minimum applies only to reports in that family.
Two-state law. The best report withholds at risk .2500; the expected-rank order has risk .3000. Nevertheless the rule wins with exact probability .700 and wins 65 of these 100 sampled draws. The state table gives the exact probabilities and losses. The scatter shows the sampled outcomes.
A short run. The rule wins 9 of 10 draws, and the paired mean difference is −.00667, favoring it in this finite sample. The exact conditional difference is positive; the paired Monte Carlo SE quantifies numerical sampling variation.
A silent common rule. Its risk is .2000 and its disclosed-error fraction is “NA: no disclosure.” Silence costs τ per pair, so a report that states nothing does not have zero reporting loss.
Identical reports. The summary reads “ties 100”: both reports have the same loss in every drawn state. Draw selection gives the corresponding state, grades and wrong counts.







Reporting loss adds wrong stated directions and withholding costs and divides the sum by all pairs. The wrong fraction uses stated pairs as its denominator. The minimum expected loss applies to reports in the search under the given posterior and loss. The paired standard error measures how the estimated difference varies across posterior samples. The model is fixed throughout.



Standalone: embed/better-on-average.html, for example ?preset=short&theme=dark.
Related applications: Comparison at matched disclosure and Selection and evaluation using posterior draws, which selects from estimated coefficients.

title: Budget and grades
text: Multiple criteria → Domain profiles

title: Budget and grades
text:
Numerical illustrations

Tighter joint budget. At k=1 and cap 3/40, the unique optimum discloses A ahead only in S. Its risk is 1/5, joint-event probability 1/20, and occupied-grade counts (2,1).
Larger joint budget. Raising the cap to 1/8 admits the report that states a direction only in C. It has risk 11/80 and joint-event probability 1/10. With more weight on C, the best report now uses two grades in C and one in S, giving counts (1,2).
Both domains disclosed. At cap 3/20, the double-positive card becomes feasible at equality. Its risk is 7/80, joint-event probability 3/20, and occupied-grade counts (2,2). The cap is inclusive.
More posterior reversals. With k=2 and cap 3/20, the best report again states a direction only in S, at risk 17/80 and joint-event probability 1/10. Changing k changes the distribution. Compare budgets within a fixed k to isolate the effect of the budget.

The chart counts the grades used in S and C. The grade table gives each site’s two grades. At every budget, the app lists all reports tied for the lowest risk and plots the counts for the first of those reports. At k=1 and zero budget, all directions are withheld at risk 1/4. At k=0, both directions can be stated even at zero budget, with risk zero.






All settings use the same nine cards, weights (1/4,3/4), and withholding costs (1/4,1/4). The joint event occurs if either domain has an error share above zero. Expected-error caps are disabled. A shared grade withholds a direction, and the error share is undefined when the report states no directions in a domain. title: Common or profile?
text:
Numerical illustrations

Aligned priorities. Both reports place A ahead of B in both domains. Each has risk 1/10, so the difference is zero.
Crossed priorities. Under equal weights and withholding cost 1/4, the common optimum withholds both directions at risk 1/4. The profile reports A ahead in S and B ahead in C at risk 1/10. Allowing that combination reduces risk by 3/20 under the same loss.

title: Site profiles
text:
Numerical illustrations

Primary saved card. Composition S has no disclosed comparisons, so its error proportion is not defined. Community C discloses 500 pairs. All forty sites occupy three profile cells.
Wider-threshold saved card. With threshold 1/10, S discloses 300 pairs and C discloses 500. Their union contains 548 distinct pairs, including 16 with crossed directions. Five of six profile cells are occupied.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text: When two true values can be equal, the treatment of equality changes the loss of a directional statement. Weak-error loss charges for a strict direction when the values are equal. Equality-neutral loss assigns zero cost to that outcome. We compare the two directions and withholding as the probability of equality changes. The crossings identify the settings at which two actions have the same expected cost. Under either loss, assigning two units to the same grade withholds their comparison.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equality .40, weak loss. Withholding costs .2500; stating A above B costs .5000 and stating the reverse costs .9000. Equality counts against both strict directions. The gray action has the lowest cost even though A is more likely to be above B than below it.
Equality .40, neutral loss. The same law now gives A above B cost .1000 and withholding cost .1500. The difference comes from consequences at equality. Along the equality slider, weak loss changes its minimum-cost action at .150; neutral loss changes at .600 and approximately .867. The open circles mark the boundaries, where competing actions have equal cost.
No equality. Both loss columns agree, and the all-withheld baseline returns to .2500. Under this law the two targets are always distinct, so charging only for distinct states changes nothing.
Equality .90. B above A has neutral cost 0, while withholding costs .0250. A strict reversal is impossible under this law, but the targets can still be equal.
Certain equality. Every neutral action costs 0. Here the targets are identical in every state, so the same-grade guard admits only withholding. The raw disclosed-pair count and the distinct mass are different quantities. A strict row has N = 1 but Q = 0: its Errors / Q reads “NA: no distinct mass”. “No disclosure” is reserved for N = 0.







The joint posterior assigns probability to exact equality. Equal posterior means or equal rounded observations do not establish that the targets can coincide. Each risk is specific to its own loss. The risks of withholding every pair coincide when both problems use the same action family and exact equality has zero probability for every criterion with positive weight.

Its field D is the distinct mass called Q_wˢ here, and R0 is the neutral all-withheld baseline. The ordinary route requires tie-free input.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text: The reported error share is the expected fraction of wrong directions under the posterior that selected the report. We can hold the report fixed and compute the same expectation under a separate reference law. The open point gives the share actually wrong at the league’s fixed true values. These three quantities can differ. The lower panels show why by comparing what changes when we sample new observations and when we draw latent values conditional on the observations already selected.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same conditional laws. The report states 152 pair directions. Both conditional expectations are .0632, and the share wrong at the fixed true values is .0526. Across repeated samples, the observed error shares can fall on either side of the common expectation.
Narrow prior, five grades. The report claims .140, while the reference expectation for that same report is .115. Their absolute difference is below the largest pair-error gap, .4981. This setting changes the prior, cost and grade cap together. Moving just the prior slider also selects a new report; each setting’s two expectations evaluate that newly selected report under both laws.
Lower cost, two grades. Only 56 pair directions are stated, with claimed share .0254. The two laws still agree. In the grade groups, pairs inside a grade are withheld, and the denominator counts only pairs stated across grades.
One grade, no disclosure. There are 0 stated directions and every share reads “NA: no disclosure.” No wrong directions is different from a defined error share of zero. The posterior-draw wrong count remains zero because this report makes no comparisons.

The lower panels separate two experiments. Observation replays keep all true values fixed, redraw estimates, and choose a new report each time. Choose a replay with the slider or select a point in the replay chart. Posterior draws keep the selected observations and report fixed, then vary latent values under the chosen conditional law. The histogram and running average describe that chosen law; adding draws reduces simulation noise without testing whether the law is correct.






We hold the league’s true values fixed across samples. Chapter 18’s conditional calibration identity applies to draws from the reference law, so the replays here do not test that identity. The pair-gap bound limits how far the two model expectations for a fixed report can differ. Its target is the difference in expectations.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text: A grade report compares every pair of sites in different grades and withholds every pair in the same grade. Sharing a grade means the report makes no statement about which site has the larger true value. The labels order grades from highest priority to lowest. They do not measure the distance between grades. Moving a site to another grade changes the corresponding cells in the matrix. The totals show how many comparisons the report states and withholds.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

A, then B to E, then F. The report states 9 of the 15 pairs and withholds 6, a share stated of .600. Every comparison involving either end is stated; the middle grade withholds its internal pairs. Moving a middle site into an end grade changes the outlined matrix cells.
Three grades of two sites. The same number of grades now states 12 of the 15 pairs and withholds only 3, a share of .800. Each grade withholds the comparison between its two sites. Together, the first two examples show how grade sizes affect disclosure even when the number of grades stays fixed.
Four sites: 1/2/2/2. The smaller report states 3 of the 6 pairs, a share of .500. A focused site button accepts a destination grade number. Enter selects the site. Use Up or Down to choose a destination, or Home or End for either boundary. A second Enter completes the move. The dashed boxes create a new grade at either end.
Beyond letter order. The report {B, D} > {C, F} > {A, E} still states 12 of the 15 pairs. Any grouping and ordering can be built. The blue and orange transposed cells represent the same unordered pair: each stated pair appears in both triangles, while the pair count includes it once.







In this example, an evaluation office plans practice-documentation visits to fictional after-school sites. The grades carry no funding consequence. The exercise counts the directions in the report the reader supplies. It does not use posterior probabilities to judge whether those directions are likely to be right. When a move empties a grade, the remaining grades keep their relative order.

postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L), pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$N # 12
canonical_postrank_grade(c(A=3L,B=3L,C=7L,D=7L,E=9L,F=9L), LETTERS[1:6]) # 1 1 2 2 3 3

title: The decision for an isolated pair
text: A report can state A above B, state B above A, or withhold the comparison. Each stated direction costs its posterior probability of being wrong, while withholding costs a fixed amount τ. The lower horizontal scale gives e_AB = 1 − π_AB, the error probability for stating A above B. A higher π_AB moves the marker to the left on that scale. The lowest line at the marker gives the action with the smallest expected loss. At an intersection, two or more actions may tie.

title: The decision for an isolated pair
text:
Numerical illustrations

π .85, τ .10. Stating A above B is wrong with probability .15, more than the .10 cost of withholding. The gray dot marks withholding as the action with the lowest expected loss. Its height varies with the withholding cost.
π .85, τ .20. The posterior is unchanged, but the withholding cost increases. The error remains .15, below .20, so the selected action is “state A above B”. Only the horizontal line moved; the posterior probability and both directional costs stayed fixed.
π .80, τ .20. The error equals .20: stating A above B and withholding have equal expected loss, labeled “equally good”. The open circle marks their crossing, and both dots receive a ring. A ring marks an action that minimizes expected loss under the specified posterior.
π .50, τ .50. Both directions cost .50 and withholding also costs .50. The summary reads “all three actions are equally good”. The crossing circles merge, while the table marks every action as minimum-cost.

The shaded area follows the smallest cost along the bottom error axis. The top scale shows the direction probability π in reverse. The marker links the two values, and the table gives the three costs at that point.






This example gives equal true values probability zero. For an isolated pair, disclose only when the posterior probability of the direction exceeds 1 − τ; at equality, disclosing and withholding tie. A shared grade withholds a direction rather than asserting equal true values. Combining many pair decisions into one coherent report adds a constraint that this isolated-pair rule does not impose.

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text: Each point represents one report. The horizontal axis gives the number of directions it states, and the vertical axis gives the expected number it gets wrong. A line of slope τ supporting the cloud from below identifies the report with the lowest posterior risk at that withholding cost. As τ changes, the points touched by these lines trace the lower convex boundary. Each vertex is attainable by a single report. Points between vertices may require randomizing between whole reports. The circles identify the best single report at each attainable number of stated pairs.

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, all reports. The touched vertex states 14 pairs and expects .3576 wrong directions, with risk .0372. The vertex table records this report and its adjacent slopes. The circles below the gray columns mark the smallest error at each attainable disclosure; only some of those circles are corners of the dashed boundary.
τ .15, all reports. A lower withholding cost selects a smaller disclosure: 13 pairs, .1692 expected wrong directions and risk .0313. A smaller τ reduces the savings from replacing a withheld comparison with a stated direction. The posterior is the same.
τ .40, all reports. The line reaches the last vertex: 15 stated pairs, .7194 expected wrong directions and risk .0480. This is the strict order. The Every report (full height) view gives the full vertical range; the close view resolves reports near the frontier.
τ .20, at most 3 grades. Only 603 reports are available. The boundary ends at 12 stated pairs and .02477 expected wrong directions; the selected report has risk .0417. The missing corners belong to reports outside this family, so they cannot be selected even when withholding becomes costly.

Each edge slope gives the additional expected wrong directions per additional stated pair. It is also the withholding cost at which both endpoint reports have equal risk. The same change points appear in The withholding cost.






The dashed segments describe mixtures of complete reports, so a point between corners need not be a deterministic report. These are fictional tutorial sites under one supplied posterior and one criterion. KRW’s related empirical figure is Figure 6 in Section V.E, “Reporting Possibilities”; the cloud here is computed from the tutorial law.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
p <- postrank_frontier(pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=c(.15,.20,.40), G_max=6L, backend="highs")
p$table[, c("tau", "N", "primary_risk", "status")]
HiGHS solves one optimization at each requested τ and returns its solver status. The browser enumerates the six-site family once to draw the whole convex boundary, including mixtures between vertices.

title: Restrictions on the report family
text: The report with the smallest risk depends on which reports the analyst allows. A cap permits any number of occupied grades up to a limit. An exact count requires every permitted grade to be occupied, and a fixed order allows only cuts between adjacent units in that order. The figure compares the best report in each family at the same withholding cost and on the same scale. Rearranging the units changes the possible cuts of the fixed order while leaving the unrestricted family intact.

title: Restrictions on the report family
text:
Numerical illustrations

Exactly six. The family contains 720 strict rankings. Its best report costs .0480, while the unrestricted reference costs .0372. Requiring every site to have its own grade forces the report to state an uncertain direction. The selected row identifies this direction and its error probability.
At most three. The capped family contains 603 reports, including reports that use fewer grades. Exactly the required number gives a smaller family of 540. Here both best risks are .0417; the shared scale makes that equality visible. Further grade restrictions can change the minimum at this fixed cost.
B before A. The declared order allows 32 contiguous reports. Its best cut costs .0379, above the unrestricted .0372. The arrows in the Declared order box modify the declared order. The dynamic program searches cuts of the declared order, and the line under the rows checks its answer against enumeration of those same cuts.
Two criteria. The four-unit example has 24 reports with every grade distinct, 75 in the unrestricted family, and 8 contiguous cuts. The exact-count row costs 7/40. The law’s table gives the criterion-specific errors and their weighted average: the orange segment now measures expected weighted wrong directions.
A dominating set. At τ = 4/9, every unrestricted best report separates {A, B} above {X, Y}, at risk 4/15. The best report with the grade cap costs 17/54 and puts X with A. The cap can make the separating rearrangement infeasible. The law panel checks the strict cross-set premise again whenever you change the price.







At a fixed withholding cost, adding eligible reports can only lower the minimum risk or leave it unchanged. The dashed mark gives the risk of withholding every pair. A family that requires several occupied grades excludes that report. Equal-risk reports are identified in the rows and the read-out, and the box of search lines states the order family’s tie rule. All examples are specified for teaching.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
sc <- postrank_expected_rank(pr_tutorial$one)
postrank_cuts(sc, pr_tutorial$one, postrank_settings(weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2, G_max=6L, exact_G=6L), rule="optimal")$risk
This cuts the expected-rank order; its result agrees with the exact-count optimum here.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text: Enumeration scores every eligible report. Dynamic programming searches among contiguous cuts of one declared order, and joint optimization searches across orders. The binary relations show which pair decisions fit into a grade report. The joint solver returns the best risk found, a lower bound, and their difference.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

DP: six sites, τ .20. The posterior-mean order admits 16 contiguous reports with at most three grades. Its current answer is {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}, with risk .0417. Enumeration checks all 603 reports in the capped family and finds the same answer here. Here the capped optimum follows the posterior-mean order.
DP: inspect one cell. The table has filled 8 of 15 feasible cells. For the current cell’s alternatives, the last cut is at b = 2. “Next cell” advances the recursion; “Fill table” shows the backtrack. The selected report remains visible above the recursion controls. Negative savings mean withholding costs more than stating those fixed-order directions.
Twelve units. The unrestricted family contains 28,091,567,595 reports. At most three grades reduces that to 523,251, while a declared order permits only 67 contiguous cuts. Equal vertical distances on the log axis represent multiplication.
A broken binary pattern. The pattern is not transitive, though completeness holds: 2 > 1. No grade vector produces this relation. The valid-pattern view enumerates all thirteen coherent reports; setting both directions to one means a shared grade, not latent equality.
Joint search: twenty units. HiGHS loads only when the joint-search control is activated for 20 league units. The output gives the status, incumbent risk, lower bound and absolute risk gap. The separate four-unit example has risks .1750 and .1500 under different grade-count restrictions, showing why a bound must keep its family.
Joint: six units. For 6 league units, the fixed-order candidate has risk .1455 from 32 contiguous reports. Press Load HiGHS and solve to compare the joint result with the exhaustive enumeration reference of .1455.







The six fictional sites use the postrank tutorial’s score-A normal posteriors. The solver uses independent normal posteriors for a simulated league. Its objective gives risk R = τ + Z/M. Divide an absolute objective gap by M to obtain a risk gap. A solver status or zero gap does not certify exact arithmetic or the posterior model. These distinctions follow theory chapter 14 and vignette m5. The R package selects HiGHS explicitly; Gurobi is its default backend and there is no automatic fallback.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk
This evaluates the displayed three-grade report directly, without invoking a solver.

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text: The posterior places all its probability on four possible orders of A, B, and C. At some withholding costs, the least costly action for each pair produces a set of decisions that no grade report can represent. We evaluate all 13 reports to measure how much risk coherence adds. Each bar separates the cost of expected wrong directions from the cost of withholding. The four states let us calculate both costs exactly, and the posterior probabilities stay fixed as τ changes.

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20. The pairwise choices cost 1/6 per pair, but the optimal coherent reports cost 11/60. Each states an extra direction with error 1/4. The two reports beneath the bars identify the additional directions and their error probabilities. The dashed line gives the pairwise lower bound, below every complete report at this setting.
τ .10. Giving everyone the same grade, {A, B, C}, costs 1/10. The outer pair can now be stated or withheld at equal cost. Some set of the minimum-cost pairwise actions is coherent, and the best bar reaches the dashed line.
τ .25. There are 3 equally good reports, all at risk 1/5. Their orange and gray segments show that the same total risk can combine different amounts of disclosure and withholding. The text retains every equal-risk optimum.
τ .30. The full order {A} > {B} > {C} has risk 1/5. Raising the withholding cost changes the choice without changing the posterior law. Keyboard selection provides each report’s risk, disclosure and directions with error above the current withholding cost.







The law is set by hand for teaching, from the theory book’s three-unit example. Each bar is one complete report: its first segment is expected wrong directions per pair, and its second pays for withheld pairs. Grades decide all pairs together, so a direction with error above the price can appear in a best report. That is compatible with the report’s overall optimality. The fractions come directly from the probabilities assigned to the four states.









TipIn postrank





The package evaluates both fixed reports under these directional errors; it does not search for them. Each returns risk 11/60 at τ = 1/5. The input records the same finite teaching law used above.
e <- matrix(c(NA,1/4,1/10,3/4,NA,1/4,9/10,3/4,NA),3,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=rep(list(c("A","B","C")),2))
input <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(e,criterion="priority",event="directional_error",zero_ties=TRUE,margin=0,source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="ABC/ACB/BAC/CBA with masses .60/.15/.15/.10",conditioning="Complete fixed finite target law"),targets=c(priority="Fictional priority; larger is higher"))
vapply(list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2),c(A=1,B=2,C=2)),function(g) postrank::postrank_evaluate(g,input,weights=c(priority=1),tau=1/5)$primary_risk,numeric(1))

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text: When the number of stated directions varies across reports, the average error share depends on how the reports enter the calculation. Dividing the expected wrong count by the expected stated count gives more weight to reports that state more pairs. Averaging the report-level fractions instead gives each report its probability weight, conditional on stating at least one direction. A third calculation assigns zero to a report that states none. We apply all three to the same counts and probabilities for a lottery over reports and for a simulation with repeated datasets.

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three outcomes. Pooled pairs give 2/5, the mean among disclosing outcomes is 1/2, and zero-imputation gives 1/3. The chance of disclosure is 2/3 and mean disclosure is 5/9. Changes to wrong and stated counts affect these summaries differently because their denominators differ. The silent outcome has an undefined fraction.
More weight on errors. Giving the error-heavy outcome more probability changes the pooled ratio to 4/7, the disclosing mean to 2/3 and the zero-imputed mean to 1/2. We normalize the weights to give probabilities for the outcomes. The number of units in each outcome stays fixed.
A complete-report lottery. The four-unit example mixes entire reports. Pooled expected counts give 1/8, while the mean report fraction is 49/400. The lottery probability weights each complete report and its disclosure. Expected weighted errors are averaged within a report before the reporting lottery is applied.
All silent. Both ratio-based summaries read “NA: no disclosure.” The zero-imputed mean is 0 because the convention assigns zero to every silent outcome. The probability of any disclosure is reported separately.
Twenty datasets. A simulated league gives pooled error .0892 and a disclosing mean .0891. The running curves and individual counts describe the averages over the selected number of datasets. The true values stay fixed while each dataset produces fresh estimates and its own graded report.







A ratio estimated from a small sample need not be unbiased for a ratio of expectations. The hand-set outcomes provide an exact single-observation example; one trajectory of simulated datasets shows variability, rather than measuring that bias. Simple rational values use fractions in the finite examples; simulated shares use the site’s decimal format.









TipIn R





A <- c(2, 0, 0); N <- c(2, 3, 0)
c(pooled=sum(A)/sum(N), disclosing=mean((A/N)[N>0]), zero_imputed=mean(ifelse(N>0,A/N,0)))
