Related applications: Expected and realized errors among stated directions, Error rates under two denominators.

title: Minimizing the largest criterion risk
text: A report with the lowest weighted average risk can perform poorly on one criterion. The minimax rule chooses the report with the smallest worst criterion risk. With two criteria, each line connects the risks for that report. The weighted rule selects the lowest line at the chosen weight. The deterministic minimax rule compares the higher endpoint of each line. Both use the same posterior, withholding cost, and report family.

title: Minimizing the largest criterion risk
text:
Numerical illustrations

w .90. The weighted best averages .0605 but reaches .2296 when only score B counts. At w .70, its weighted risk is .0882 and its worse endpoint is .1378. The price panel compares each selected guarded report with the weighted best under that same loss.
w .30. Both rules choose {A, B, C, D} > {E, F}; its larger expected criterion risk is .0944. The peak panel gives the largest minimum weighted risk and the weight at which it occurs.
Score B only. Two weighted reports share the smallest risk. Their worst endpoint risks are .1996 and .2113; both identities, dashed alternative and complete criterion profiles remain visible.
Book low and Book high. In the restated two-unit law, the weighted rule changes from withholding at risk .2500 to stating A above B at risk .1500. The table gives both risks and the larger risk for every report.
Book minimax. The guarded rule continues to withhold, with maximum .2500. Under Zero error weight, the same .2500 guard remains because a zero error weight does not remove a guarded criterion.
Certain opposition. Exactly two grades exclude withholding. The highest point of the lower envelope is .5000, while deterministic minimax is 1.0000. This makes the gap between those two quantities visible.







Note



For the minimax calculation, we first take the expected loss on each criterion and then take their maximum. Averaging the worst loss in each posterior state would define a different decision rule. The chart clips lines that extend beyond the displayed range. The table and keyboard view give the full values. In a restricted family, the maximum of the weighted minimum can be lower than the deterministic minimax risk.

The package’s synthetic minimax example also withholds every pair; it uses its own units.

source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package="postrank", mustWork=TRUE), local=TRUE)

title: Optimal reports along the criterion-weight path
text: For a fixed report with two criteria, weighted risk moves along a straight line between the two criterion risks. The lower envelope of these lines gives the smallest risk at each weight. Its intersections locate exact changes in the best report. Within each resulting interval, the report, disclosure count, and criterion-specific error shares stay fixed while weighted risk varies. The boundary table lists the optima where lines tie.

title: Optimal reports along the criterion-weight path
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The selected report states 9 pairs. Its expected wrong shares are .0177 on score A and .0267 on score B. The interval table and lower envelope identify the weights for which this report is optimal.
Lower A weight. The best report states 12 pairs and favors score B’s ordering of the conflicting sites. Both criterion shares stay fixed across the interval while their weighted average changes.
Higher A weight. The report again states 12 pairs, with {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}. Its expected wrong share on score B is .237. The two twelve-pair reports disagree about which sites rank above the others.
Score B only. At the endpoint, 2 reports share the smallest risk. The expected wrong shares on score A are .200 and .215. The boundary data keep their identities and differing profiles. The first interval has zero width in the display.
No cap. The unrestricted calculation searches all 4,683 reports. The current equal-weight report still states 9 pairs, but the complete path can differ away from the selected weight.
Higher withholding cost. The uncapped current report states 14 pairs. The interval table retains every short interval; both criterion-share paths use these same boundaries.







Note



The path uses independent normal posteriors for the six fictional sites. When an interval next to zero is at the scale of numerical rounding and both reports tie at zero within the tolerance, the chart shows them as an endpoint tie. The detailed table retains the computed interval and boundary results. Each point on the lower envelope is the minimum for its own weight, which is the horizontal coordinate.

title: Posterior profiles on multiple criteria
text:
The same sites can rank differently on reading growth and family engagement. The site with the largest posterior mean on one measure may rank lower on the other.
The panels show the posterior means and marginal intervals on their original scales. Lines connect the same site across the two orders. Selecting a pair gives the probability that the proposed direction is wrong on each criterion. This comparison can show strong support for opposite directions or weak support on either measure. The priority order also depends on whether a higher or lower score calls for an earlier visit.

title: Posterior profiles on multiple criteria
text:
Numerical illustrations

Thirty sites. There are 397 opposing pairs among 435 pairs. The highest posterior mean belongs to a different site on each criterion. Alignment by unit labels displays each unit’s criterion-specific profiles.
Six sites, B–C. The error of stating B above C is .007 on score A and .961 on score B. The complete list has 3 opposing pairs. A very likely direction on one criterion can be very unlikely on another.
Six sites, B–D. The errors are .002 on score A and .760 on score B. The difference remains visible when both panels use the same order of site labels.
Reverse score B. Lower score B now means higher priority. The error of stating B above C on the oriented score becomes .039. This change reverses the direction that counts as higher priority without changing the underlying scores.
Wider intervals. The marginal level becomes 95%, while the 397 opposing pairs stay the same. Interval level changes the displayed uncertainty bands, not the supplied posterior probabilities or mean orders.







In the six-site example, score A measures standardized reading growth and score B is a standardized index of family engagement. Higher scores ordinarily imply earlier visits to document site practices. The example assigns no funding. Each interval describes one marginal normal posterior. The released marginal summaries for thirty sites leave the joint draws and the distribution of a composite undetermined.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text: An error budget caps the expected share of wrong stated directions on a criterion. A report can carry little weighted risk and still exceed that cap. The plot shows each report with positive disclosure at its two criterion error shares. We use the same weights and withholding cost to compare the best report that passes the budgets with the best report overall. For a report that withholds every pair, we test the expected wrong count against the budget times the stated count.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text:
Numerical illustrations

Loose budget. With equal weights and score B’s budget at .03, only 3 reports qualify. The original optimum is one of the three. It states 9 of 15 pairs and has risk .0933.
Tight budget. At .02, 2 reports qualify. The best states 8 of 15 pairs and has risk .0939; the other report withholds every comparison. The ring marks the optimum in the reduced family.
Exactly three. Keeping the .02 budget while requiring exactly three grades leaves 0 reports feasible. Allowing fewer grades makes it possible to withhold every comparison again.
Both budgets. Requiring an expected wrong share at most .02 on each score also leaves 2 reports. Both count-form checks and their slacks are reported; a report must pass both rows.
Zero weight. Score B has zero error weight but still has its .10 budget. The best feasible report has risk .0906. Its largest single score-B error is .240, for E above F, while its average is .0267. A budget on an average allows some individual errors above it.
No budget. The score-A-only best has risk .0417 and expected wrong share .237 on score B. The cross marks this unconstrained best; the older At most .15, At most .10 and At most .05 presets retain the same score-A-only comparison.







The example uses independent normal posteriors for six fictional sites. The budget limits an expected share under those posteriors. A report that withholds every direction has an expected wrong count and stated count of zero, so it satisfies the count inequality when the grade cap allows it. Its error share is undefined. The app checks the budgets by enumerating the six-site reports. The package’s typed-coefficient interface does not accept these budget settings.



Standalone: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets, for example ?preset=both&theme=dark.
Related applications: A common grade report for two scores · Criterion-specific excess risk of a common report.

title: A random-criterion representation of weighted risk
text: Consider a fixed grade report and draw one criterion, with chances given by the error weights. Evaluate the whole report on that criterion. The average risk over these draws equals the weighted risk computed directly. The draw applies to all units and all pairs, preserving their joint distribution within the chosen criterion. The report is already fixed when the criterion is drawn.

title: A random-criterion representation of weighted risk
text:
Numerical illustrations

Weighted report. Both calculations give risk .0933. The criterion contributions are .0453 and .0480. Select a criterion column to inspect its whole vector. Report 1/1/1/1/2/3 stays fixed.
Certain opposition. The two directions each cost .5000, while withholding costs .3000. Both criteria distinguish the units with certainty. The same criterion choice applies to both units and every reported pair.
Three actions tie. All 3 actions cost .5000. Other reports share the weighted minimum even though their risks differ by criterion. Each report is evaluated before a criterion is drawn.
Two against one. The cheaper direction costs .3333, the reverse .6667, and withholding .4000. A certain two-against-one split can favor disclosure. The adjacent one-third boundary preset retains both actions sharing the minimum instead of treating equality as a strict preference.
Zero error weight. The cheaper weighted direction costs 0, although the ignored criterion’s own risk is 1.0000. Its selection chance is 0, so this branch contributes nothing. The column still shows how the report fares on that criterion.
No-cap coherence. Among all 4,683 reports, 1/2/2/3/4/5 states 14 pairs with risk .1275. It states A above C with weighted error .3803 and B above D with .3813, both above τ .35. There is no grade cap in this example.







The criterion draw is independent of the targets conditional on the supplied information. Its probabilities are the weights in the loss. In postrank, a strict direction counts as wrong when the target values are equal. The link to KRW’s strict-count objective requires matching the law, targets, orientation, units and report family, as well as the affine and equality conditions of that result.









TipIn postrank





The fixed default report reproduces the two calculations; small floating-point rounding differences do not change their algebraic identity.
library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=1L,C=1L,D=1L,E=2L,F=3L), pr_tutorial$two, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), tau=.2)
sum(c(.5,.5)*ev$criterion_risk); ev$weighted_risk



Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=coherence&theme=dark.
Related applications: Opposing criterion directions · A common grade report for two scores.

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text:
Weighting errors on two criteria and comparing a weighted sum of their values can yield opposite directions for the same pair.
Error weights determine how much a wrong direction on each criterion costs. Composite coefficients determine how much each target contributes to the combined value. At A = (1, −2) and B = (0, 0), a direction with less weighted error can therefore run against the order of the equally weighted composite. We compare the reports under both objectives, holding the withholding cost and available reports fixed.

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Different targets. The criterion-direction costs are .2500, .7500 and .3000 for forward, reverse and withholding. The composite costs are 1.0000, 0 and .3000. One objective picks 1/2; the other picks 2/1.
Rescale the second criterion. In Data and exact values, A’s composite value becomes .250. Its preferred direction flips. The criterion-direction cost .2500 stays the same. The positive multiplier applies to every unit, while error weights and composite coefficients keep their separate roles.
Composite equality. Both strict composite directions cost 1.0000. Withholding costs .3000. Each criterion still distinguishes the units, but their composite is equal; a shared grade withholds rather than asserting that equality.
Two reports, same disclosure. Data and exact values shows the evaluations of all 75 reports. Criterion directions choose 1/2/2/3 with risk .1417; the composite chooses 1/1/2/3 with risk .0333. Both disclose 5 pairs. Both columns evaluate each selected report under the two objectives.
Transform the whole law. Exponentiating every finite input preserves the criterion best report and its risk .1417. The composite now selects 1/1/2/2 with risk .0667. The complete criterion best-report sets before and after remain visible under the same settings.
Rescale the Normal composite. The first composite mean is .635. We compute it assuming independence across the six sites and their criteria. Computing the composite uncertainty requires the same assumptions about dependence.







All examples are synthetic supplied laws. Composite coefficients stay nonnegative and sum to one, matching the package interface. A positive multiplier changes the contribution of a criterion to the composite. A strictly increasing transformation leaves the ordering within that criterion intact. Choosing which risk to minimize depends on whether the report concerns individual criterion directions or the composite. The thirty-site marginal releases leave the joint law undetermined.









TipIn postrank





The code computes composite scores from the posterior means, with weights as the composite coefficients. The package divides by the supplied scale, so a second-criterion scale of ten corresponds to a multiplier of .1.
library(postrank)
postrank_composite(pr_tutorial$law$means, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), scales=c(score_A=1,score_B=10))

title: Sensitivity to costs, weights and grade restrictions
text:
Changing the withholding cost or the criterion weights changes how the report is evaluated. Changing the grade cap changes which reports may be chosen.
For the live path, we vary the withholding cost while holding the posterior, weights and available reports fixed. The grid repeats the comparison for the listed combinations of costs, caps and weights. We use the criterion error shares and number of stated pairs to compare what the reports say as settings change. The archived cases provide results at the recorded settings.

title: Sensitivity to costs, weights and grade restrictions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The best report states 9 of 15 pairs. Its wrong shares are .0177 and .0267 on scores A and B. The exact path gives its interval and all returned equal-risk alternatives at the boundary costs.
A higher price. The report states 11 pairs; score B’s wrong share is .115. A larger withholding cost can favor additional statements, even though some statements are less certain.
A still higher price. The report states 12 pairs, while score B’s wrong share falls to .0575. Disclosure cannot fall along this fixed-family exact path; a criterion-specific wrong share can move either way.
At most two grades. The best report states 8 pairs with risk .0939. The cap table holds the price and weights fixed. A higher cap retains every previously allowed report, so the minimum risk can only stay the same or fall.
Thirty-site archive. Recorded disclosures include 131, 276, 305 and 312 pairs. These dots describe the saved solves at their recorded prices. Their spacing does not locate the exact transitions of a continuous path.
Tutorial archive. The package’s prepared sensitivity analysis has 7 settings, changing one setting at a time. In the live grid, we evaluate a fixed reference report under every combination.







Each row reevaluates the reference report under that row’s loss, even when the cap rules it out of the search. The thirty-site archives use joint posterior draws and fixed settings. The live Gaussian example gives the intervals and boundary reports along its path. The archive points show the original solver status and gap. The R example reads the tutorial results, which vary one setting at a time.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
s <- readRDS(system.file("extdata/cached/tutorial_sensitivity.rds", package="postrank", mustWork=TRUE))$value
s$table[, c("setting_id", "risk", "N")]

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text: KRW award λ for a correct direction, charge one for a wrong direction, and assign zero payoff to withholding. postrank instead charges one for a wrong direction and τ for withholding. A conversion between λ and τ makes the two objectives select the same reports when they use the same posterior, orientation, units, and report family and the target has no ties. The six-site example compares the two scales for a single pair and for a complete report. KRW’s interpretation of the reward also makes assumptions about what readers know.

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ .25 (KRW’s card) gives τ .20 and a direction-probability cut of .80. For a pair on its own, both rules state a direction beyond that cut. Both choose {A} > {B} > {C, D} > {E} > {F} among the six-site reports.
λ .08 gives τ .0741. The audience-share row gives the corresponding share of informed readers assumed in KRW’s model.
λ .10 gives τ 1/11 and cut 10/11. The best report is {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}; a shared grade leaves its units uncompared.
λ .50 gives τ 1/3 and cut 2/3. The dashed and solid lines give the reverse- and forward-direction costs, respectively.
λ 1 gives τ .50 and {A} > {B} > {C} > {D} > {E} > {F}. The two direction cuts meet, and the stipulated informed-audience share reaches zero.
τ .40 works from the other scale: λ is 2/3. The three outcome rows give the payoff and cost transformations.

The conversion changes the scale of the loss under the same posterior and feasible family. It supplies no evidence about posterior calibration. A grade report must give transitive directions, so an isolated pair’s cutoff cannot serve as a separate constraint on each reported direction. The audience share comes from the assumptions in KRW’s behavioral model. The example contains no observations of readers.

title: KRW’s archived reward path
text: KRW’s archive gives a card at each hundredth of the reward λ from zero to one. The cards generally state more pairs as the reward for a correct direction rises, although disclosure falls at some steps. The figure evaluates each fixed card using the released pair probabilities and shows which comparisons change from the preceding grid point. KRW chose the cards with their archived probabilities and solver tolerances, which matter when comparing this path with exact optima under one posterior.

title: KRW’s archived reward path
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ .25: published race card. The baseline card states 1,324 pairs, with E/N .136. Grade counts appear on a logarithmic scale. DR divides expected errors by all possible pairs.
λ .08: first race split. Genuine Parts stands alone above the other 96 firms. Its standard error is smaller than AutoNation’s, despite AutoNation’s larger estimate. Risk .07406 is just below its own all-withheld reference; the comparison needs the extra decimal.
λ .01: one grade. The card at the first positive λ states no direction, so E/N is undefined. The table also includes the archived card at λ zero, where postrank risk is undefined.
λ .30: statements and silence. Against the preceding grid row, 830 pairs become stated and 92 become withheld. The comparison uses the adjacent archived rows each time.
λ .98: disclosure dip. Between λ .97 and .98, the number of stated comparisons falls from 4,620 to 4,614.
λ 1: end of grid. DR and E/N coincide at .268 because every pair is stated. The complete Purples matrix uses a different scale: it shades stated errors, unlike the Blues direction probabilities in the heat-map app.







KRW’s code selected the grid cards using their archived probabilities and solver tolerances. The app holds those grades fixed and evaluates them with the released postrank probabilities. The baseline race card is in Figure 7, and the gender card is in Figure 14 (§VIII). Figures 5A and 6 are in §V.E, and Figure 10A is in §VI.B.

title: KRW’s race and gender report cards
text: KRW’s cards report which firms have larger contact gaps by placing firms in ordered grades. The grade assignments and expected error rates can change with the target or the reward λ for a correct direction.

title: KRW’s race and gender report cards
text:
Numerical illustrations
Grade 1 is highest on the chosen target. The card states directions between grades and withholds them within a grade. A correct direction earns λ, a wrong direction costs 1, and withholding pays 0. DR divides expected errors by all pairs. E/N divides them by the number of pairs the card states.

Published race card. The card states 1,324 of 4,656 pairs, with expected wrong share E/N .136. Its risk .1818 comprises .0387 for errors and .1431 for withholding. In this card, comparisons between distant grades have lower expected error rates than comparisons between adjacent grades.
Reveal grade 1. The remaining bands stay in place. As each grade is revealed, its firms enter the disclosure and between-grade tables.
Sort by estimate. State Farm moves 69 rows inside its grade. Changing the row order changes no reported direction. Genuine Parts and AutoNation illustrate why estimates alone do not determine the card.
λ .08: first race split. The risk .07406 is slightly below all withheld, .07407. The extra decimal prevents rounding from hiding that distinction. The displayed card is still an archived KRW grid card.
Published gender card. It states 731 pairs. Both ends of its signed scale are contact gaps; three stated directions are more likely wrong than right. The note identifies these firms and probabilities.
One grade. Nothing is stated. E/N is NA: no disclosure, meaning undefined; the app draws no E/N bar.

The precision plot places each firm’s original sampling SE beside its grade. The table identifies each firm. KRW’s prior depends on precision. Firms with uncertain estimates can share the middle grade while having very different contact gaps.






KRW’s code selected the grid cards using their archived probabilities and solver tolerances. The app holds those grades fixed and evaluates them with the released postrank probabilities. title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text:
The minimum-risk report with at most three grades places F and I in the same grade, even though the posterior strongly favors F above I.
Requiring F above I can change comparisons involving other schools. To measure the added risk, the browser searches the same report family again with that direction required. The tertiles and a four-grade report based on cuts of the posterior mean order also state F above I. These comparisons show how much the outcome depends on the grouping and on which reports the search considers.

title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text:
Numerical illustrations

F above I shows posterior probability .9999 for that direction. Among the 175,099 reports that state it, the lowest risk is .064087, just above the unrestricted minimum of .063774 in the same family.
I above F requires the reverse. The best report stating that direction has risk .112261. That risk includes all the report’s stated and withheld comparisons.
The tertiles state it uses the two tertile cuts. This fixed report states 48 pairs with risk .082255, so stating F above I does not require a fourth grade.
The higher-cost optimum sets τ to .45. The optimum itself now states F above I and has risk .143197.

The table ranks the three reports with the lowest risk in the same family. The best report stating F above I ranks second. The school selectors accept pairs of distinct schools.
The four-grade search considers only cuts of the posterior mean order. It admits some reports that the three-grade search excludes and excludes others that the three-grade search admits. Both use the same posterior, τ, and weight, so the risks are comparable. Several restrictions can contribute to withholding the same pair.
Data: California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde). This deliberately spread twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools; prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated. CDE source conditions apply (https://www.cde.ca.gov/re/di/cr/index.asp); the data are not relicensed and are provided as is without warranty. No CDE endorsement is implied.
The pair comparison concerns chronic absence in this subset. When the report places two schools in one grade, it leaves their relative absence rates unstated. The calculation uses its own reporting loss. California’s Dashboard colors, school quality, causal effects, statewide optimality, and calibration each require evidence beyond this comparison.

This call reads the probability of F above I from the original case-study input.
library(postrank)
e <- postrank_pairwise(pr_case_cde$input)$e
1 - e[6, 9, 1]

title: School tertiles and minimum-risk grades
text:
Two cuts in the order of posterior mean chronic absence divide the twelve schools into grades.
Moving a cut can change both how many comparisons the report states and which schools it compares. The browser evaluates those cuts and searches all reports with at most three grades. It uses the same posterior and withholding cost τ for both. Grade 1 identifies the schools reported to have lower chronic absence.

title: School tertiles and minimum-risk grades
text:
Numerical illustrations

Tertiles puts four schools in each of three grades. The report states 48 pairs, with 1.829 expected errors and risk .082255. The minimum-risk report states 45 pairs and has risk .063774.
Archived grades puts the cuts after positions 3 and 9. The resulting grades match the archived report, which states 45 pairs at risk .063774. Every pair has the same relation in both reports.
One boundary puts both controls at position 6. One distinct boundary gives two grades, 36 stated pairs and risk .091293.
Higher withholding cost raises τ to .45. The optimum now states 47 pairs and has risk .143197. The changed-pair table identifies the resulting relation changes.

The cuts follow the posterior mean order. The full search also considers assignments that depart from that order. The displayed average-error bound applies to the report that minimizes risk at the displayed τ. It places no separate threshold on individual comparisons in the tertiles. Both reports use the same loss, so their risks can be compared even when they state different numbers of pairs.
The dots and intervals summarize each school’s posterior. Schools in the same grade appear in posterior mean order, but the report leaves their relative chronic absence rates unstated.
Data: California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde). This deliberately spread twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools; prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated. CDE source conditions apply (https://www.cde.ca.gov/re/di/cr/index.asp); the data are not relicensed and are provided as is without warranty. No CDE endorsement is implied.
The example compares ways to report chronic absence among these twelve schools. California’s Dashboard colors follow separate status-and-change rules. The loss comparison provides no measure of school quality or causal effects, and assessing statewide performance or calibration would require other evidence.

This call uses the supplied posterior to evaluate the fixed tertiles at τ .20.

g <- pr_case_cde$reference$actions$observed_rate_tertiles

title: postrank Explorer
text:
When two schools have similar estimates, a strict ranking still puts one above the other. An ordered grade report can place both schools in the same grade and leave their comparison unstated. To evaluate either report, we count the comparisons it makes and use the posterior distribution to estimate how many of those directions are wrong.
The examples use methods implemented in the postrank R package. The package takes a posterior or pairwise probabilities as input. The examples cover simulated data and released studies of firms, schools, and counties. In the five Domain profiles applications, each domain has its own grade column. The examples show when the columns can be selected separately and when a limit on errors across domains changes the best combination.

title: postrank Explorer
text:
Applications by topic


Uncertainty. How sampling error affects ranks and how the posterior changes the comparison. The normal–normal example shows that estimates with different precision can change order after shrinkage.
Grade reports. How a report balances expected mistakes against unstated comparisons. Withholding cost sets the cost of leaving a pair unstated relative to stating the wrong direction.
Reporting rules. How tiers, evidence flags, and posterior cuts compare. Matched-disclosure comparisons hold the number of stated pairs fixed so that rules can be compared by their expected errors.
Multiple criteria. Two ways to report on several outcomes for the same units.

Common grades. The two-score example shows how one grade column performs on both scores. Other examples compare weights, error budgets, and minimax risk.
Domain profiles. The common and separate cards show what changes when domains can have different grades. Separability and dependence show when a joint limit changes the choice. Resolution and forty fictional sites show how much detail each domain retains.

Cases. Firm contact gaps, school chronic absence, and historical county outcomes. The school example evaluates tertiles and minimum-risk grades under the same posterior.
Tools. Build a report from supplied posterior summaries or revisit a released case. The case-report tool exports the data source, targets, settings, and report.


The catalog lists the applications by category, concept, and data source. Application 1.3 is the third example in Part 1. Each page includes worked examples with preset settings. The standalone versions also run offline from the downloaded site folder.

title: postrank Explorer
text:
Numerical verification
The checks compare earlier examples with results from postrank 1.1.0 and independent base-R calculations. They also run the exported R workflows with postrank 1.2.0. For the multidomain examples, they compare feasible reports, optimal reports, and ties with results from postrank 1.2.0 using exact fractions. The live finite-law profile examples search every candidate in their stated sets. The forty-site example displays results saved from a separate analysis. The repository records the sources, fields, licenses, and checksums for the released data.
Each numerical illustration is checked against the values displayed at its stated settings. The result identifies the family of reports searched. Agreement in these examples establishes that the implementations agree for the inputs tested. Assessing calibration requires evidence about how the posterior model performs outside these calculations. The test inputs and comparison code are in verification/ and r-export/.

title: A common report for Alabama county outcomes
text: A single grade report compares Alabama counties on two historical outcomes, household income and incarceration. Grade 1 indicates higher income and lower incarceration. Changing the weight changes the relative cost of mistakes on the two outcomes. The map links each county’s grade to the marginal intervals in the table.

title: A common report for Alabama county outcomes
text:
Numerical illustrations

“Equal weights.” Crenshaw County is the only county in grade one. Montgomery and Russell share grade five. The expected error shares among stated comparisons are .0520 for income and .172 for incarceration.
“Income only.” The report states 1,769 of 2,211 pairs. The incarceration error share rises to .349. Under “Income .80”, the incarceration and income shares are .305 and .0305, respectively. Each risk uses the loss for its own weights.
“Fixed income D1.” At equal weights the archived D1 grades have risk .1906, compared with .1998 for D2. The corresponding map is available below the main comparison.
“Color counties by this report.” Choose an archived report or edit the grades. The table gives each county’s grades and intervals and shows how the stated comparisons differ from archived P. “Incarceration only” gives shares .312 on income and .0873 on incarceration.

The browser searches cuts of one order, based on the counties’ weighted average posterior ranks. At the original cost and cap, the search reproduces P at equal weights, D1 for income alone, and D2 for incarceration alone. The archived solver status and bounds apply to those original runs. The commonality table reports how much risk the original common report adds for each outcome compared with a report optimized for that outcome alone. Its bounds apply to the original loss and the full family allowed by the grade cap.






The estimates pool race and gender for cohorts born in 1978–83 whose parents were at the 25th income percentile. The outcomes are household income in 2014–15 and incarceration on April 1, 2010. The grades describe associations for those cohorts. Present-day need, eligibility, and the causal effect of growing up in a county would require other evidence. The two separate fits give marginal distributions for each outcome. title: School reports at matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

At the tertiles’ disclosure shows all 34,650 reports at N = 48. The tertiles have the fewest expected errors, with E = 1.829. The next report has E = 1.909.
Between feasible disclosures selects N = 46. No single report in this family states exactly 46 pairs, while the lower hull reaches H = .4551 by a mixture with weight .500 on the more-disclosing report.
A lower mixture selects N = 30. The hull value is .005174, using weight .167 on the more-disclosing endpoint.
Other cuts, full range places cuts at 1 and 2. The selected report states 21 pairs and expects 1.116 wrong directions; the enlarged axis shows the complete ranges at every disclosure.

Only three groups of four can reach 48 stated pairs. A randomized rule that averages 48 stated pairs must choose only reports at that maximum. The tertiles already have the fewest expected errors among those reports, so randomization cannot improve on them at 48.
The mixture weight is the probability of choosing the report that states more pairs. The histogram and the table available by keyboard give the full error distribution. A shorter table lists the five reports with the fewest expected errors.

title: School-report changes along the withholding-cost path
text:
Numerical illustrations

The usual setting uses τ .20. The optimum states 45 pairs in groups of sizes 3, 6, 3.
Past the last interior boundary uses τ .45. The optimum states 47 pairs in grades of sizes 4, 5, 3. The table names every pair whose relation changes.
The early boundaries keeps the slider at its low end. The exact boundaries near .000162 and .000263 lie below that minimum but remain in the tables, including the step to 27 pairs.
The upper endpoint reaches τ .50. The path still states 47 pairs, and the chart retains all 13 archived solves.

The posterior, criterion weight, and set of reports with at most three grades stay fixed along the path. Under those conditions, a higher τ cannot reduce the number of pairs stated by an exact optimum. The number can rise even as the report drops or reverses particular comparisons.
Each point’s risk uses its own value of τ, so risks at two steps evaluate different losses. At a boundary, the table lists the equal-risk reports and the tolerance used to identify ties. text:
Numerical illustrations

λ 1, flat line gives slope 0. The full order 1/2/3/4/5/6 has DR .0480 and expected correct minus wrong per pair .904. KRW call the minimizing grades Condorcet ranks. The separate 97-firm panel evaluates the fixed grid card.
λ .25 gives slope 3. Both objectives choose 1/2/3/3/4/5, with postrank risk .0372. The ring marks the full grade assignment.
τ .25, whole grid checks every report at 49 values of τ. Both objectives return the same set of reports at 49 of 49 values. The table gives the corresponding λ and grade vectors.
λ .08 gives τ .0741 and 1/1/2/2/3/3. More pairs share a grade when a correct direction earns less.
τ .40 moves the other slider: λ becomes 2/3 and the full order returns. Arrow keys on the figure read every report, including reports away from the best line.

The identity holds for the same posterior probabilities, target orientation, units, and report family. For every report, postrank’s risk equals τ plus the product of one minus τ and KRW’s risk at the matching λ. The residual records numerical rounding in this identity. A tolerance determines which computed risks count as equal.
KRW chose the archived card using their original probabilities. The fixed-card evaluation uses the released postrank probabilities, so it cannot establish that the card minimizes risk under those probabilities. title: Firm-pair probabilities and report-card blocks
text: Each cell gives the posterior probability that the row firm’s contact gap is larger than the column firm’s gap. Darker blue indicates stronger support for that direction. The threshold shows which directions would minimize loss if each pair were decided on its own. The grade blocks show what the archived report actually states. Some high-probability directions lie within a grade and are withheld. Some directions between grades fall short of the pairwise threshold. Select a cell or choose two firms to read their comparison above the matrix.

title: Firm-pair probabilities and report-card blocks
text:
Numerical illustrations

All direction probabilities. The Blues legend reads “Pr(row truly higher)”. Arrow keys move through every cell, including the diagonal. Each cell names both firms and gives their relation in the card.
Above the threshold. At λ .25, the corresponding withholding cost is τ .20. The strict pairwise rule would state 1,575 pairs whose favored direction has probability above .80. Other cells fade, while the gray diagonal continues to mark self-comparisons.
Add the card blocks. Orange hatching marks 575 confident pairs withheld within a grade. Purple outlines mark 324 stated pairs whose error exceeds τ. The discrepancies can arise from requiring one coherent report, even with no grade cap.
λ .50 blocks. The threshold admits 2,994 pairs. Of these, 49 are withheld by the card; 545 stated pairs have error above the current τ. Varying the reward changes both the threshold and the selected archived card.
Gender blocks. The target is the signed male-name contact advantage. Negative gaps favor female-named applicants. Both row-above-column directions retain this signed orientation.

title: A common report for race and gender gaps
text: A common report assigns the same firm grades for race and gender contact gaps. The race weight determines how much errors on each gap contribute to the loss. The scatterplot shows the selected grades. The risk chart evaluates the common report and KRW’s two published cards at the same weight and withholding cost.

title: A common report for race and gender gaps
text:
Numerical illustrations

“Equal weights.” At the original cost, the common report’s risk .2455 is below the risk of withholding every comparison. Both published cards have higher risk than withholding every comparison.
“Race .80.” The race card crosses the withholding line near race weight .69. “Gender .80” shows the opposite crossing near .29.
“Color firms by this report.” The risk uses the current cost and the selected card’s original grades. Select a firm in the scatterplot or table, or use the selector, to read both marginal intervals.
“Most grades allowed in the live order search.” For each cap, the app gives the number of reports searched and lists the reports tied for the lowest risk. Grade one ranks highest. A shared grade leaves a comparison unstated.

The browser combines each firm’s average posterior ranks with the current weights and searches cuts of the resulting order. At the original equal weights, cost, and cap, it reproduces the archived result from a search over all capped reports. The archived status, bound, and gap apply to that original search. Each published KRW card was chosen under its own objective. Its risk here answers how the fixed card performs under the current loss. See the original report card for its interpretation.






The separate race and gender fits give marginal intervals and expected losses for each gap. Estimating how the gaps vary together in the posterior would require a joint fit. The scatterplot instead shows variation across firms in the historical experiment. These experimental data do not describe firms’ current conduct. title: Signed and absolute gender-gap targets
text: A firm with a large female-name contact advantage can rank low on the signed scale and high on the absolute scale. Each line connects the same firm’s grades under the two targets.

title: Signed and absolute gender-gap targets
text:
Numerical illustrations
The two reports use different posterior pair probabilities. For each target, the app orders firms by expected rank and searches cuts of that order. To compute probabilities for absolute gaps, the transformation applies to the gaps throughout the posterior distribution. Signed means or signed direction probabilities alone cannot recover the absolute report.

Both target-specific cards. Both searches allow at most 4 grades at withholding cost τ .20. Each result is labeled “optimal within this order.” A different order can admit different grade reports.
Every changed pair. The “Complete list of changed unordered pairs” keeps every relation that changes from the signed report to the absolute report. A direction can appear, disappear or reverse. Each row names both firms and shows the wrong-direction probability under the posterior for that target. The signed and absolute risk values answer different questions.
All firm summaries. “All firms in released ID order” keeps all 97 firms together. The table keeps the supplied means and central 90% intervals for both targets, their expected ranks, and their chosen grades.

The dots and intervals describe individual firms. The grades depend on the pair probabilities, order, grade cap, and withholding cost. The report leaves the direction unstated for two firms in the same grade. The absolute-gap probabilities come from the public postrank data, which supplies separate signed and folded distributions.
Both precision plots use the original sampling SE of the signed estimate. In the plot of absolute gaps, that SE describes the precision of the original signed estimate. Firms in the middle grade can still differ in their contact gaps.

title: Criterion-specific excess risk of a common report
text: A criterion may have higher risk under a common report than it would have under grades chosen for that criterion alone. We call the difference the commonality cost. Each connector joins the separate minimum to the risk of the common report for that criterion. Both evaluations use the same set of possible reports and withholding cost. Equal error weights can still give unequal costs. The larger examples use optimization bounds saved with the original reports.

title: Criterion-specific excess risk of a common report
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The excess risks are .0490 on score A and .0145 on score B. Each connector joins the criterion-specific optimum to its common-report evaluation. The comparison table keeps each criterion’s risk separate from its wrong share.
Score A only. The common report is score A’s own best, so score A has zero excess risk and score B has excess risk .1481. Score B still has its own comparison; a zero error weight does not remove that criterion from the display.
w .70. The common report becomes {A} > {B, C, D} > {E, F}: the excess risks are .0253 on score A and .0563 on score B. Moving a weight changes the objective used to select the common report.
Score B only. Two common reports tie. Score A has excess risk .1580 under one and .1697 under the other; score B has zero excess risk. Both common reports and both of score B’s own optima are shown, with their equal-risk tolerance.
Thirty sites, higher price. The archived common report states 276 pairs. Snap’s cost is .4455, and its expected wrong share among those stated directions is .784. The cost interval comes from optimization bounds.
Thirty sites, lower price. The common report withholds every direction, yet each criterion could prefer a report of its own. Costs are .0895, .0749 and .1022 for poverty, frl and snap, respectively.







The package writes this risk difference as Δₖ. It measures the cost of a common report under the chosen loss. Judging the weights or the consequences of using the report requires additional information. The thirty-site results come from archived analyses of posterior draws. Their intervals are bounds on the minimum from the search. We show the separate grade vectors where the archive includes them.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
cc <- postrank_commonality_cost(postrank(pr_tutorial$two, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), tau=.2, G_max=3, backend="highs", report_card=FALSE, fragility=FALSE), backend="highs")
cc$table[, c("criterion_id", "cost_lower", "cost_upper")]

title: Opposing criterion directions
text:
Two criteria can favor opposite directions for the same pair. To identify those pairs, the matrix compares the error probabilities for both directions on each criterion.
The bars give the weighted costs of stating either direction or withholding the comparison. These costs can be similar when the criteria agree within each state but the order changes across states. They can also be similar when the criteria disagree about a pair whose values are known. The finite examples distinguish these two possibilities. A common grade report must also reconcile the chosen direction with its other comparisons.

title: Opposing criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, B–C. The equal-weight costs are .4841 for B above C and .5159 for C above B. The map has 3 opposing pairs. Withholding is cheaper for this pair on its own, but these actions do not yet form a common grade.
Thirty sites. There are 397 opposing pairs. For the selected pair, the smaller expected directional cost is .3652. Each criterion has equal error weight; the table keeps its separate errors visible.
Certain opposition. The two directions each cost .5000; withholding costs .2000. Here the smaller directional cost is also the statewise conflict quantity. The additional boundary preset shows every action sharing the minimum when withholding has the same cost.
Uncertain agreement. The smaller posterior directional cost is still .5000, but statewise γ is 0 in each state. The criteria agree within every state; uncertainty about which state holds creates the directional cost.
Zero error weight. The opposing pair stays on the map, while its cheaper direction costs 0 and the reverse costs 1.0000. The criterion with zero weight still favors the reverse direction, but its error adds nothing to the weighted cost.
Latent equality. In Data and exact values, the first criterion’s two directional errors are .6000 and .9000, both above one half, yet it prefers the smaller one. The other criterion prefers the opposite direction. Both weighted directions cost .7500; comparing errors with their reverse detects this disagreement even with equality mass.







A strict direction counts as wrong when the two values are equal. Comparing the two error probabilities therefore identifies the preferred direction even if both probabilities exceed one half. The map includes criteria with zero weight. In each state, γ is the smaller cost of the two strict directions. Across states, uncertainty about the true values can raise the expected cost, and the two sources need not separate uniquely.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
pr_tutorial$two$e["B", "C", ]

title: Pairwise errors from joint posterior draws
text: A posterior draw gives the values of all units and criteria in one joint state. We estimate the probability of a wrong direction by counting the states in which it is wrong and dividing by the number of draws. The package’s 32-state example shows what happens if we shift the values for one unit by a row. The unit has the same marginal values, but the shift changes which values it is compared with. Shifting all units together reorders complete states and preserves the full-sample error rates.

title: Pairwise errors from joint posterior draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Original states. Among the 32 retained states, placing 001 above site-B is wrong 8 times on need_A and 32 times on need_B. The empirical error shares are .250 and 1. Each complete state specifies the order of all three units on both criteria.
Shift one unit. Moving site-B’s whole two-criterion vector forward cyclically changes the need_A count to 7 times and its share to .219. The need_B count remains 32 times. The raw marginal values have only been reordered; the joint pairing has changed.
Move states together. Applying the same shift to every unit restores the original full-sample counts: 8 times and 32 times. Each state still contains the same values, so every full-sample error share stays the same.
Short prefix. Only 8 retained states now enter the estimates. Even a shift of complete states can change which draws appear in the first 8 rows.
Unshifted pair. The pair 001 and site C contains neither shifted unit. Its counts remain 0 times and 25 times, with need_B share .781. Changing a third unit’s pairing cannot change this pair’s comparisons.
Full cycle. A full cyclic shift returns every source vector to its original row, with counts 8 times and 32 times again. The source table retains all original unit and criterion coordinates.







The original states are independent draws from the same synthetic normal law. An error share of zero means that no retained draw shows the event. Its posterior probability can still be positive. The shifted comparisons reuse the original sample to show how pairing across units affects the estimated probabilities.









NoteIn postrank





library(postrank)
e <- postrank_pairwise(postrank_toy)$e
e["001", "site-B", ]  # need_A .25, need_B 1

Related applications: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities · Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities.

title: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities
text: An error budget caps the expected share of wrong stated directions. A report may pass that budget when we use estimated probabilities and fail it under the exact probabilities. A uniform error bound lets us use a tighter estimated budget to find reports that definitely pass, and a looser one to retain every report that passes. We check the bound and both claims about the report sets separately. A separate fixed-size simulation shows how often a bound of this kind can hold over repeated draws from the same law.

title: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Estimated pass. For A above B, the estimated wrong share is .200 and the exact supplied-law share is .300. The budget is .25. The estimate passes and the exact probability fails. The number line shows the tighter threshold .15 and looser threshold .35.
Negative inner. The signed inner threshold is −.05, even though the estimated wrong share is 0. Replacing this threshold with zero would wrongly admit A above B. The all-withheld report still passes the count-form tests, with no defined wrong share.
Exactly two. Requiring two grades removes all-withheld. The inner family has 0 reports; the exact family also happens to be empty here. Their separate counters matter: an empty inner family alone would not establish exact infeasibility.
Radius too small. The proposed radius is reduced to .05 with the exact law unchanged. The coefficient checks read “no,” and an inner member fails the exact budget. The report that passes the tighter estimate but fails the exact budget is shown in the table.
Raw comparisons. With advisory tolerance removed, its coefficient check reads “no.” At the default radius, the tiny raw excess explains why the strict check fails while the tolerant comparison passes. The actual inclusions are separate tests, not consequences of accepting a soft tolerance.
Fixed-S IID. The simulation uses 1,000 complete states drawn from the independent normal posteriors for six sites. Score B has error weight 0 but remains protected by its .03 budget. Requiring exactly two grades gives an empty inner family while the exact family remains nonempty.







The two-unit example specifies the exact and estimated probabilities directly. In the simulation, the chance that all estimated coefficients fall within the bound is at least one minus α across repeated samples of the same size from the same law. This probability describes the numerical estimates under that law. Compliance under the model is still determined by the exact expected wrong share. The thresholds can be negative.



Standalone: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities.
Related applications: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets · Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities.

title: Quantities not identified by pairwise probabilities
text:
Pairwise probabilities are enough to calculate the additive expected risk of a fixed report. To know how often every statement is right, we also need to know how the errors occur together.
In the finite examples, we change how the two criteria’s states are paired while holding fixed each criterion’s full distribution for the two units. A fixed report then has the same additive risk under every pairing. Its chance of being right on all criteria can change, as can the probability of a direction on a composite. The composite depends on the magnitudes of the targets as well as their order.

title: Quantities not identified by pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Together: each disclosed direction has additive risk .5000. For A above B, the probability that both criteria are right is .5. The displayed state masses belong to entire arrays; they do not describe independently drawn criterion columns.
Opposite: the additive risk stays .5000, while both the forward composite error and the probability of being right on every criterion become 0. The composite is always positive, although the criteria point opposite ways within each state. The full table retains all reporting actions.
Halfway: the all-criteria probability is .250. The wrong-count distribution changes with the coupling even though its expectation and every report’s additive risk stay fixed. Error weights and withholding cost remain separate controls; changing them changes the loss.
One zero error weight: the probability of zero weighted wrong count is .5, while all-criteria correctness is 0. A criterion given zero error weight still belongs to the all-criteria event. The weighted wrong count can be zero even when a direction on that criterion is wrong.
Select withholding: the wrong or correct fraction reads “NA: no disclosure.” Because the report states no directions, no direction can be wrong.
Five statements: the fixed report’s mean weighted fraction correct is .870, but the probability all its statements are right on every criterion is .750. It makes 5 statements. The second state has weighted wrong count 2.600; the criterion grid gives its whole-state probability and contribution to the average.







Note



In these examples, larger target values mean higher reporting priority. The state editor changes the association between criteria while preserving each criterion’s distribution. The complete report table shows which report has the lowest risk and how the selected report fares under each loss. Marginal pair probabilities alone leave the joint events and the composite posterior undetermined.


Open standalone, for example ?preset=opposite&theme=dark.
Related applications: Composite targets and criterion directions, Opposing criterion directions.

title: A common grade report for two scores
text: A common grade report assigns one grade to each of the six sites. In this example, a wrong direction contributes to reporting risk with weight w on score A and 1 − w on score B. Withholding a pair costs τ once. The lines between posterior means show where the two scores order the sites differently. The two error profiles show how the selected common grades fare on each score.

title: A common grade report for two scores
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The report states 9 pairs at risk .0933. Its expected wrong shares are .0177 on score A and .0267 on score B. The outlined pair errors show why low-cost isolated directions need not appear in a coherent report.
No cap. Searching all 4,683 reports still gives the same 9 stated pairs. The same pairs remain withheld because the grades must be coherent even without a cap.
A-heavy. Giving score A more weight restores the three blocks {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}, stating 12 pairs. The profile shows the consequence for each score separately.
Score A only. The report follows score A’s order between its blocks. On score B an expected .237 of its stated directions are wrong, although score B contributes no error cost.
w .70. The common report keeps {B, C, D} together; score B’s expected wrong share is .115. Its pairwise relations differ from those at equal weights.
Score B only. The best report is tied with another report. The expected wrong share on score A is .200 under the first and .215 under the other; both reports and full profiles appear.







Note



The example uses independent normal posteriors. Grade one has highest priority, and pairs in the same grade are left unranked. The error bound is for the expected average across the stated pairs. Individual directions can have higher error probabilities. Each set of weights defines the loss used to choose and evaluate the report.








TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
two <- postrank(pr_tutorial$two, weights = c(score_A=.5, score_B=.5), tau=.2, G_max=3L, backend="highs")
get_grades(two); get_profile(two)[c("criterion", "E_over_N", "risk")]

Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost.

title: Reasons for a withheld comparison
text: When two units share a grade, the report leaves their direction unranked. Select a pair to see what it costs to state either direction on its own and what it costs to require that direction in a complete report. The posterior stays fixed for both comparisons. Several tests can account for the same withheld pair. The changed-pair table shows how requiring one direction also changes other comparisons in the report.

title: Reasons for a withheld comparison
text:
Numerical illustrations

Coherence: the six-site report withholds A–B even though its isolated forward cost is below the withholding cost. The minimum-cost complete report stating A above B has risk .1019, with a change of +.008513. Removing the cap does not remove this difference. The table lists the other directions that change and their contributions to the risk difference.
Certain conflict: each criterion is certain about B–C, but they point opposite ways. Requiring B above C produces risk .1667, with a change of +.025000. The reverse direction is a separate search with a different full report and cost.
Uncertainty: the two criteria agree within every stipulated state. Their directional expected costs are .4000 and .6000, while each known state’s smaller directional cost is zero. Here the isolated direction is costly because the states disagree about which unit is higher.
Fixed order: B above C is feasible along the declared order, but its minimum-cost report has risk .3167. The unrestricted family provides a separate comparison. Under Indivisible block, requiring those two units to stay together makes both directions infeasible.
CDE subset: all 523,251 reports with at most three grades belong to the declared search. Forward and reverse requirements are evaluated separately. The schools were chosen to span the range for this illustration. The result applies to these schools under the fixed statewide prior.
KRW fixed order: the search contains 147,537 contiguous-cut reports. Relaxing the cap keeps the expected-rank order fixed. The reports are new postrank calculations for that order, separate from KRW’s archived cards.







Note



The extra risk measures the cost of the required direction under the given posterior and report family. It can reflect more than one reason for withholding. The case views give the data sources and assumptions. CDE source conditions apply. KRW is noncommercial use only under CC-BY-NC, with no endorsement implied.


Open standalone, for example ?preset=fixed-order.
Related applications: Opposing criterion directions, A common grade report for two scores, Posterior summaries in a grade report.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text: An analyst can select a report under one posterior law and evaluate it under another. We hold the selected report fixed while changing one site’s evaluation mean or all of the evaluation standard deviations. For each change, we compute the risk of the same report under both laws. We then compare its evaluation risk with the lowest risk attainable under the evaluation law in the same report family. The difference from that minimum is evaluation regret.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same laws. The selected report has risk .0417 under either law, and evaluation regret is 0. The plotted intervals and means coincide; the largest pair-error gap is also 0. Changing the evaluation law shows how far the two assessments can diverge.
Move C upward. The frozen report’s evaluation risk rises to .1360, while the evaluation-best report has risk .0542. Their difference, .0817, is the regret. The chosen reports change 3 pair decisions. The table separates the two evaluations of each report.
Wider evaluation law. The frozen report now has risk .0779, yet regret remains 0. It is still best in the family under the evaluation law. A change in the risk of a report does not by itself imply that another report should replace it.
C +.40, no cap. Evaluation regret is .0108. Both optimizations now search the larger family. The family labels identify the same set of eligible reports for both calculations.
Small change, new report. There is 1 changed pair decision. How the bounds are calculated gives the pair-error radius of .0132. Regret is only .0008, beneath the uniform bound .0263. A small objective gap can coexist with different grade vectors.







Both laws use independent normal distributions specified for the example. The regret bound adds two quantities: twice a uniform bound on the difference in risks across laws and a bound on the selection-law optimization gap. Both bounds apply to the whole common family. We enumerate every report, so the selection-law optimization gap is zero. Increasing the number of draws under either law would leave any difference between the two laws in place.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$weighted_risk # .04165164

title: Selection and evaluation using posterior draws
text: In each repetition, we draw from a specified posterior and estimate the pairwise probabilities from those draws. We select a report using the estimates. We then hold that report fixed and score it twice, once with the selection draws and once with the exact probabilities. The estimated risk can be above or below the exact risk. A separate calculation compares the selected report with the exact-law optimum in the same family. This comparison measures the cost of the selection itself.

title: Selection and evaluation using posterior draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Own draws. The graph reads “33 look worse” for the displayed selections. Those reruns have higher risk on their own draws than under the exact law. Choosing other tied reports can change the count. The selected run’s gap of −.00061 means its own draws give the lower risk.
Looks worse. Another selected report from the same experiment has a positive discrepancy. Its gap is +.00072 even though it minimizes risk for its own estimated probabilities.
More draws. With 4,000 draws per run, the followed gap is −.00025. The cloud and coefficient radius describe the remaining numerical variation. Realized errors need not shrink on every step.
Tighter family. Search the 603 reports with at most three grades. The followed gap is +.00102. Both evaluations still refer to that run’s same selected report. The gray intervals show that a bound can be much larger than the observed gap.
Both scores. The two scores receive equal weights. The followed gap is −.00322. The discrepancy radius now averages each score’s largest pair-error discrepancy with those same weights.

The gray intervals bound the absolute difference between the two risk evaluations for each selected report. Regret compares that report’s exact-law risk with the exact-law minimum. The regret bound allows for numerical optimization. Two grade assignments can differ even when their risks are close.






The example uses independent draws from normal posteriors specified for six fictional sites. The exact risks come from those same distributions. The separate package example selects a report on one fold and evaluates it on the other. Both folds contain draws from the same posterior, so that exercise cannot assess how the model would perform on new observations.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
cf <- postrank_crossfit(postrank_toy, settings=postrank_settings(weights=c(need_A=.6,need_B=.4),tau=.25,G_max=3L), backend="highs")
cf[c("mean_optimism", "mean_abs_optimism")]
This reproduces the separate package fold example, not the browser’s six-site draws.
