title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text: The pairwise actions that minimize expected loss need not fit into a single grade report. Consider three units A, B, and C with independent normal posteriors. Moving B’s mean changes the probabilities for pairs that include B and can change which directions are worth stating at the chosen withholding cost τ. The density panel shows the three posteriors. The other panels compare the risk of deciding each pair separately with the risk of the best grade report. Their difference is the additional risk of requiring one ordered partition for all three pairs.

title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Middle at 1.00. A–B and B–C are withheld separately, while A above C has probability .921 and is stated. Transitivity of shared grades contradicts that direction. The minimum coherent risk is .1728. Both optimal reports, named in the read-out, resolve the conflict by stating an additional direction; the strip under the curves shades their extra cost.
Middle at .50. B moves closer to C. The choices now form {A} > {B, C}, with risk .1410. The same report attains the minimum from deciding each pair separately.
Middle at .80. The mean is just outside the shaded band and the report reaches risk .1589. Additional displayed digits resolve probabilities near the decision boundary.
Middle at 1.00, τ .10. The withholding cost decreases. The best report is {A, B, C}, risk .1000; it withholds the confident outer pair too. The pairwise choices remain incompatible with a grade report, but the minimum-risk coherent resolution has changed.
Middle at 1.00, τ .25. The threshold falls to .75, below .760. Every pair is stated, the shaded band vanishes, and {A} > {B} > {C} represents the pairwise choices. The density panel is unchanged because τ affects the loss rather than the posterior.







Sharing a grade is transitive. If A shares a grade with B and B with C, the report must also withhold the comparison of A and C. Kline, Rose and Walters describe the conflict with the separate pair decisions as a “Condorcet cycle in indifferences.” These are posteriors set by hand for teaching. The browser evaluates every report of the stated family, lists equal-risk optima and gives their tolerance; the band is an aid to reading the picture, while compatibility is checked directly against the reports.



Standalone: coherence, for example ?omega2=.81&tau=.20.
Related applications: The decision for an isolated pair, Coherence in a finite three-unit example.

title: Expected and realized errors among stated directions
text: A report that states N directions has expected error share E/N when N > 0, where E is the sum of the error probabilities of the stated pairs. The probability that all of the statements are correct depends on how the errors occur together. The draws show how the realized wrong count varies for the same report. When the report withholds every pair, the error share is undefined because N is zero.

title: Expected and realized errors among stated directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Start without draws. The report states 14 of 15 pairs, and its expected share wrong is .0255. The blue cells give the stated-pair errors. The optimality badge is reassessed after changes to the grades or eligible family.
Best report, draws. Across 100 draws, the mean count is .360 wrong directions per draw, with mean share .0257; the expected count is .3576. The matrix crosses the directions wrong in the final draw. The histogram counts draws, while the line shows their running average.
All withheld. The share reads “NA: no disclosure.” There are no statements that could be wrong, so the probability that all are correct is 1. The error share has no denominator. The drawn values remain visible, and the histogram records no wrong statements. The best-report button evaluates an alternative report on the same draws.
Three-unit law. The expected share wrong is 7/40, while B above C has error 1/4, above τ. The exact all-right probability is 3/4, with union lower bound 13/20. The final draw’s wrong share is 1/2.
Another coupling. The expected share stays 7/40, but the exact all-right probability becomes 13/20, meeting the same union lower bound. As the coupling varies, the order table, draws and zero histogram bin change together.

The same draws can be used to score several reports. For a fixed report, changing τ affects only the withholding charge. Its expected wrong count stays fixed.






The badge “E ≤ τN applies” appears only for an exact optimum of the shown family when that family includes the all-withheld report; for any other report the badge says only whether E ≤ τN holds. Every report also shows the defined risk/count diagnostic, including when nothing is stated: E ≤ τN exactly when risk is at most τ. The six-site draws use independent normal latent values: their all-right values are Monte Carlo estimates, while the finite-law values and union bounds are exact. Both posteriors are stipulated; the joint-event interpretation and finite example follow the theory book, chapters 6 and 10.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1,B=2,C=3,D=3,E=4,F=5), pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)
ev[c("N", "E", "E_over_N")]



Standalone: open the app, for example ?draws=100&seed=1.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost · Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Mixtures of frontier reports
text: A lottery between two complete grade reports can achieve an expected number of stated pairs between the counts of those reports. The diamond gives the mixture’s expected wrong count at that level of disclosure. The square gives the smallest expected wrong count among single reports with the same number of stated pairs, when one exists. Every realized report remains coherent because the lottery selects a complete grade assignment. The examples compare how much the lottery can accomplish in unrestricted and restricted families.

title: Mixtures of frontier reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, mean 10. The mixture selects the report stating 12 pairs with probability .50 and the report stating 8 pairs otherwise. The average error count is .01714. No single report states exactly this many pairs. The diamond is an average over the two reports.
Six sites, mean 9. The more-disclosing report now has chance .25. The mixture expects .01332 wrong directions; the best single report at this disclosure expects .1597, a gap of .1464. The square and diamond share the same horizontal coordinate.
Six sites, mean 12. The selected point is a corner with .02477 expected wrong directions: no mixture is needed. Moving the mean-disclosure slider changes the lottery, while moving the withholding cost changes the supporting line and its best report.
Four units, mean 4. With two criteria, the quantities are expected weighted wrong directions. The mixture has 19/40 against the best single report’s 7/10, a gap of 9/40. Its two complete reports each have chance 1/2.
At most 3 grades, mean 9. The family has 603 reports and ends at 12 stated pairs. The unrestricted endpoint conclusion is not guaranteed for this family. The fixed-order example in the box on the endpoint at τ = 1/2 gives a different reason that a restricted family can miss the unrestricted endpoint.







The half-cost endpoint requires the full report family and no latent ties on positive-weight criteria. The small fixed-order figure shows the boundary for that order. The six sites and the finite laws use posteriors specified for the examples.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=2,F=2), c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=3,F=3))
vapply(g, function(x) postrank_evaluate(x, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.20)$E[1], numeric(1))
This evaluates the two complete reports at the mixture’s endpoints. Their error counts appear in the vertex table. The average point weights those counts by the two selection probabilities.



Standalone: embed/frontier-mixtures.html, for example ?preset=tb16.
Related applications: The error–disclosure frontier · Reporting risk and withholding cost · Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution.

title: The number of ordered grade reports
text: An ordered grade report groups the units and specifies the order of the groups. Thus, the full family contains every strict ranking and every report that gives some units the same grade. A cap on the number of occupied grades reduces this family. A fixed-order family contains only reports formed by cutting that order. The curves compare the sizes of these families on a logarithmic scale. The small examples show which changes to the grouping or order produce a distinct report.

title: The number of ordered grade reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three units. There are 13 ordered grade reports but only 6 strict rankings. In the small examples, some reports group letters, while others give each letter its own box. Swapping the positions of occupied boxes changes which directions are stated.
Six units. There are 4,683 reports in all. The cap permits 603, the exact grade count permits 540, and cuts of one declared order permit 32. The capped family includes reports with fewer occupied grades, which explains its larger count than the exact family.
Eight units. All reports reach 545,835, compared with 6,051 under the cap and 128 along one order. Colors and dash patterns identify the families even when their counts are close. The legend shows counts at the selected number of units, and the labels at the right show counts for twelve units. The arrow-key reader and table give every count.
Twelve units. There are 28,091,567,595 reports in the full family, while the cap leaves 523,251. The hollow squares mark problem sizes encountered elsewhere in this collection. Counting those possibilities does not require generating every report.
An empty exact family. The small example has 0 reports: the requested number of nonempty grades exceeds its number of units. An empty family has no logarithmic height, so its count stays in the table of exact counts.







A report that follows a declared order can cut only between adjacent units in that order. This example has no equal-score blocks. These counts describe the number of eligible reports. The posterior risks and the work required to find the best report depend on the particular problem and algorithm.



Standalone: report counts, for example ?n=8&G=3.
Related applications: Grade reports as pairwise decisions, Reporting risk and withholding cost.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text: Correcting one unit’s posterior mean or standard deviation can change comparisons between units whose posteriors remain fixed. Dropping a unit can have the same effect. The report assigns grades jointly, so a change to one unit can move the boundaries between other units’ grades. The two cards share the same scales. The matrix and list compare which directions the reports state or withhold. When a unit leaves the population, we compare only the pairwise decisions for the remaining units.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correct a mean. The first result names 2 of 10 changed pairs between untouched units, D–E and E–F. The correction moves one site down while rearranging boundaries among other sites. The relation table distinguishes new disclosures from new withholding decisions.
No correction. The original posterior is retained and 0 of 10 untouched pairs change. The two cards describe the same report. Varying the corrected mean identifies the next boundary change.
More uncertainty. Under a tighter grade cap, raising one site’s posterior SD changes 6 of 10 untouched pairs. The ten pairs still have the same posterior probabilities. The new grade assignment changes how the report treats six of them.
Drop a unit. Removing a site changes 1 of 10 remaining pairs. The relation comparison excludes the removed site and compares directions, rather than numerical grade labels.
Drop U15 from the league. The original card has grade sizes 1, 12, 15, 2; the new card has sizes 9, 17, 3. Among the remaining units, 107 of 406 relations change: 62 newly withheld and 45 newly stated. The expected-rank order is recomputed after removal, and each report is optimal within its own order, with no grade cap.
Two scores, drop C. Equal-weight scores A and B use all reports. Removing C changes 2 of 10 remaining pairs: A–B and A–D become stated. Both marginal-card views show the same common grades; neither score alone chose them.

The two single-score views let the reader correct one marginal posterior. The two-score and league views remove a unit. Each comparison holds the withholding cost and grade policy fixed.






The example uses independent normal posteriors and changes only the marginal for the selected score. Refitting a model to corrected data could also change other marginals. Dropping a unit retains the remaining marginal distributions but changes the population, pair count and possibly the declared order. The display compares relations on common IDs and checks unchanged pair probabilities for every criterion. An excluded unit is unassessed here, not assigned the lowest grade.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
original <- postrank(pr_tutorial$one,tau=.2,G_max=3L,backend="highs",fragility=FALSE)
get_grades(original)
This reproduces the original score-A report.



Standalone: open the app, for example ?preset=league-drop.
Related applications: Posterior summaries in a grade report · Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text: A wrong direction costs one and a withheld comparison costs τ. The posterior risk of a grade report averages these costs across all pairs. If E is the expected number of wrong directions, M the number of unordered pairs, and N the number of directions the report states, this risk is R_τ = E/M + τ(M − N)/M. The first term charges for expected mistakes and the second for withheld comparisons. We use the same τ to evaluate the report entered by the reader and the best report in the selected family.

title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, at most 3 grades. The best of 603 reports states 12 of 15 pairs, with risk .0417. The matrix says “2 (A and B; E and F)” for below-τ pairs still withheld. Stating those directions would save risk if the pairs could be handled separately. A complete report under the cap would also have to change other comparisons, at greater cost.
τ .20, no cap. The best of 4,683 reports states 14 of 15 pairs, with risk .0372. Only C–D stays withheld. The change-point strip identifies subsequent changes in disclosure.
τ .40, no cap. The strict order states 15 of 15 pairs; risk .0480 consists entirely of expected wrong directions. The all-withheld bar always ends at τ, because it pays that cost on every pair.
τ .30, no cap. The best report stays the same while its risk becomes .0438. A larger τ changes the charge for every withheld pair. Risk comparisons use the same current τ.

Choose a Quick report or enter grade labels in site order. The bar just below the entry evaluates that fixed report at the current τ. An entered report outside the selected family is identified explicitly; it may beat the capped optimum without belonging to its comparison family.






We use the normal posteriors for score A at six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial. For these posteriors and the costs on the slider, the uncapped optimum states exactly the pairs whose error is below τ. The risk is an expected cost per pair. The chance that at least one direction is wrong is a separate joint probability. The risk formula follows the postrank theory book, chapters 10–11.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk
This scores the displayed capped report directly. The package’s solver-based tutorial also reports a floating-point correction to the lower bound; direct fixed-report evaluation needs no solver.



Standalone: open the app, for example ?tau=.2&cap=3&stage=2.
Related applications: The decision for an isolated pair · Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text: Each row of the report card shows a unit’s posterior mean and marginal interval, and color identifies its grade. A comparison across grades states a direction. A comparison within a grade is withheld. In the table, each cell below the diagonal averages the error probabilities for the stated pairs between those grades. It measures the expected share of wrong comparisons in that group of pairs. Showing one grade at a time makes it possible to see which comparisons enter as grades are added.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites. The card states 12 of 15 pairs, a share .800, with risk .0417 and expected share wrong .00206. Adjacent-grade comparisons have average errors .0024 and .0038. The purple cells compare these errors with those between distant grades. The diagonal marks withheld pairs. Grade means appear separately above the matrix.
Reveal by grade. Only Grade 1 is drawn initially; the table says “With one grade shown there is nothing to compare yet.” Displaying another grade introduces the corresponding between-grade comparisons. Later grades retain their colored bands and numbers while their rows are hidden.
Thirty sites. The card states 303 of 435 pairs, with risk .1603 and expected share wrong .121. Adjacent-grade shares are .2019, .1672 and .0640. These are averages for the stated pairs. The joint probability that every unit in one grade exceeds every unit in another would require a separate calculation.

Expected rank averages a unit’s position under the posterior, with the top position first. Sorting by posterior mean can rearrange rows within a grade. The comparison of two sites in that grade remains withheld, and the report retains the same risk.






These synthetic posteriors are taken as given. Grade 1 declares priority; in the poverty example it means the highest synthetic need. The intervals describe individual units, and their overlap does not determine grades. In these cards the least certain stated comparisons are between adjacent grades. The larger example keeps one expected-rank order and chooses where to cut it into grades; its optimum is restricted to that declared order.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
one <- postrank(pr_tutorial$one, tau=.2, G_max=3L, backend="highs", fragility=FALSE)
one$fit$evaluation[c("G", "N", "M", "disclosure_rate")]



The larger dataset is the poverty criterion of pr_example_gaussian, an analytic posterior law. The card follows the package’s report-card plot. The between-grade table follows Figure 10 and Section VI.B of Kline, Rose and Walters.
Standalone: open the app, for example ?data=thirty&tau=.25&cap=4&order=mean.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost · Expected and realized errors among stated directions.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text: The risk of a fixed report changes linearly with the withholding cost. The slope is the share of pairs the report withholds. The lowest line at each τ gives the smallest risk in the selected family. Where the lowest line changes, the reports on either side of that point tie. A cap on the number of grades can remove some of these reports and change the path. The low-cost view shows the first transitions, including the range over which the best report withholds every pair.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overview. The unrestricted best report states 14 pairs, with risk .0372. The capped comparison gives .0417. Each faint line gives the risk of a fixed report. The heavy line traces the lowest risk, and the bands below show the costs over which each report attains it. Arrow keys identify the reports on the envelope. Complete path gives their exact intervals.
Before the first bend. The report states 0 of 15 pairs, and risk equals the withholding cost .0005. The low-cost strip includes the all-withheld report that an overview starting farther right would miss. The left boundary is a limit, since the cost is positive.
Small cost, coherent report. The best report states 12 of 15 pairs, including 2 directions whose error exceeds the withholding cost. The list under Complete path gives the error probability for each newly stated direction. These choices are made jointly, so the path cannot be read as a collection of isolated-pair thresholds.
Exactly at a bend. 2 reports share the smallest risk. Both neighboring segments include the shared endpoint; the read-out shows the first report under the stated equal-risk tolerance. Moving just beyond the bend changes which line is lowest.
Three-grade cap. At the larger cost the capped report still states 12 of 15 pairs, with risk .0817; the unrestricted comparison gives .0480. Restricting the available grades changes the decision problem even though the posterior and the price of withholding are the same.







The site posteriors are normal and specified for this example. A separate panel shows targets with equal means. In that example, some reports minimize risk at a single cost. The path includes them even though they occupy no interval of positive length.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=2L,C=3L,D=3L,E=4L,F=5L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$weighted_risk # .03717176
The call evaluates the displayed report at a fixed cost.



Standalone: the τ path, for example ?tau=.005&zoom=low.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost, Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text: The same report can have a low expected error rate over all possible pairs and a much higher rate among the directions it states. Both rates use the same expected wrong count E. KRW’s discordance rate, DR, divides E by all M unordered pairs, and E/N divides it by the N stated pairs. For positive N, DR = (N/M) × E/N, where N/M is the fraction of pairs the report states. We compare the two rates for a synthetic report and KRW’s archived race card.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .25. The synthetic best report states 14 of 15 pairs, a share .933. DR is .0238, while the expected share wrong among stated pairs is .0255. The two rates are close because almost all pairs are stated.
KRW setting. The race card states 1,324 of 4,656 pairs, a share .284. DR .0387 divides the expected wrong count by all pairs; E/N .136 divides it by the stated pairs. Its KRW risk is −.0227 and its postrank risk is .1818, evaluated on the released probabilities.
All pairs stated. The synthetic report states all 15 pairs. Both rates are .0480 because their denominators coincide. The race card remains fixed as the controls change; its title records the costs at which it was chosen.

The rounded identity uses an approximation sign because multiplying rounded rates need not reproduce the rounded product exactly. Both rates are expectations over pairs. The chance of at least one error in the report depends on the joint distribution of those errors.






KRW’s archived card statistics and the evaluation on released pair probabilities agree at the displayed digits. The released probabilities differ slightly from KRW’s archived probabilities. We use the archived grade assignments as given and evaluate them under postrank’s loss. Its risk below the cost of withholding every pair implies that its expected error share is below that cost at this setting.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1,B=2,C=3,D=3,E=4,F=5),pr_tutorial$one,weights=c(score_A=1),tau=.25)
ev[c("N","M","E_over_M","E_over_N")]

title: Domain profiles
text:
Multiple criteria → Domain profiles

Domain profiles give sites a separate grade for each outcome. A site can rank higher on composition need and lower on community need. The two grades describe those separate priorities.
P.1 compares common and separate grades. P.2 considers when grades can be chosen separately, P.3 examines errors that overlap across domains, and P.4 varies the budget for errors across both domains.
The first four examples evaluate every candidate under a fully specified fictional distribution. The forty-site example shows grades and risk summaries from an earlier fictional analysis.





P.1
Common or profile?
Compare one shared grade column with two domain columns under the same posterior and loss.
standalone





P.2
Separate or joint?
Separate domain choices can minimize additive loss. A joint error limit can make their combination infeasible.
standalone





P.3
Error overlap
The same domain posteriors can lead to different best profiles when their errors overlap differently.
standalone





P.4
Budget and grades
A looser error limit can increase reporting detail in one domain and reduce it in another.
standalone





P.5
Site profiles
Read two grades for each of forty fictional sites and compare the directions stated within each domain.
standalone

title: Error overlap
text: Multiple criteria → Domain profiles

title: Error overlap
text:
Numerical illustrations

Coincident failures. The two directions each have error probability 1/10, and they fail together. Stating both gives probability 1/10 of at least one error, below the cap 3/20. That card alone minimizes expected loss at 1/10.
Disjoint failures. The marginal probabilities remain 1/10, but the probability of at least one error rises to 1/5 if the report states both. The cap rules out that card. Two cards tie at risk 7/40, each stating one positive direction and withholding the other.
Independent domains. At overlap c=1/100, the probability of at least one error when stating both is 19/100. This exceeds the joint cap even under independence, so the same two cards tie for the lowest risk.
At the joint cap. At c=1/20, the probability of at least one error when stating both is exactly 3/20. A probability equal to the cap is allowed, so that card is feasible and uniquely optimal.







The example uses a complete fictional distribution with equal domain weights, withholding cost 1/4, and zero thresholds. The joint event occurs if either domain’s error share exceeds its threshold. A shared grade leaves a direction unstated. When several feasible cards have the same lowest risk, the app lists all of them and shows one first. The exact calculation applies to this distribution and these candidates.









TipIn postrank





The R script reproduces the example with postrank 1.2.0 and gmp.
source("profile-dependence.R")
result <- profile_dependence()
result$summary



Source: postrank multidomain decisions.
Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=coincident&theme=dark.
Related applications: Separate optimization under additive loss, A common grade report for two scores and Criterion-specific expected-error budgets.

title: Separate or joint?
text: Multiple criteria → Domain profiles

title: Separate or joint?
text:
Numerical illustrations

Dependent domains, separate choices. Coincident reversals give a feasible product of all nine cards. Both domains prefer A ahead, with total risk 1/10, even though their targets are dependent.
Different dependence, same minimum. Disjoint reversals leave each domain’s distribution and weighted losses unchanged. With the joint cap disabled, stating A ahead in both domains still gives the unique optimum at risk 1/10.
Zero loss weight in S. All three S columns have the same weighted loss, and C still favors A ahead. The three resulting cards tie at risk 1/10. Their unweighted losses in S differ.
Independent domains with a joint guard. The feasible family has three cards and fails the product condition. The two domain minima sum to 1/10, but the card that combines them has joint-event probability 19/100, above the cap 3/20. The two feasible optima each state a direction in one domain, at risk 7/40.
Joint guard with coincident failures. Four feasible cards form a product of two columns per domain. The best card states A ahead in both domains. Its risk and joint-event probability are both 1/10.

With independent reversals, zero S weight, and an active cap, a feasible card still reaches the lower bound of 1/10. Some combinations of weighted minima exceed the cap, but only one needs to pass to reach the bound. Errors in S still count toward the cap when its loss weight is zero.






The fictional distributions have the same marginals. The calculation evaluates the nine cards in this example, with expected-error caps disabled and the joint cap set separately. A shared grade leaves the direction unstated. If the supplied law approximates another posterior, feasibility under that posterior requires a separate check.









TipIn postrank





The R script reproduces all twelve settings with postrank 1.2.0 and gmp. It uses the public results to identify each domain’s feasible columns and weighted minima.

result <- profile_separability()
result$summary

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text: Quartiles and deciles split firms into nearly equal groups by posterior mean, keeping exact score ties together. We compare these reports with archived cards using Kline, Rose and Walters’s measures of discordance and informativeness. Both calculations use the released pair probabilities. In each example below, the selected archived card makes fewer expected wrong directions per possible pair and provides more information than the fixed tiers. The comparison evaluates reports that have already been chosen.

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race quartiles, card λ .60. The quartile point has DR .1696 and I .4185. The ringed card has lower DR, .1678, and higher I, .4336. The size patterns show how the card’s grade boundaries differ from the nearly equal quartiles.
Race deciles, card λ .82. Deciles move to DR .2271 and I .4550, while the selected card reaches .2243 and .4589. The deciles disclose more pairs than the quartiles. The selected card still has lower DR and higher I.
Gender quartiles, card λ .64. Under the signed male-name contact-gap target, quartiles have DR .1978 and I .3621; the card gives .1908 and .3875. These coordinates concern a different target from the race comparisons.
Gender deciles, card λ .80. Deciles give DR .2525 and I .4042; the card gives .2373 and .4078. The comparison depends on the selected λ. The selected card need not improve both coordinates at every grid setting.







KRW discuss deciles and quartiles in §IV.B and Figure 2C, and reporting possibilities in §V.E and Figure 6. The diamonds show the fixed tiers. The curve joins cards that KRW selected using their archived probabilities. We recompute each card’s coordinates with the released probabilities without rerunning that search. KRW use τ̄ for informativeness. For gender, the target is the signed contact gap.

Provided as is, without warranty. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.









TipIn postrank





x <- postrank::pr_case_krw$alternatives$race
b <- postrank::postrank_cuts(setNames(x$summaries$means[,1],x$entity_ids),x,postrank::postrank_settings(weights=c(race_signed=1),tau=.375,G_max=10),direction="descending",rule="quantile",G_b=4,method="posterior_mean")
b$evaluation[c("N","E_over_N","primary_risk")]

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text: A quantile-tier rule sorts units by their estimates and divides them into groups of nearly equal size. It places every unit in a higher tier above every unit in a lower tier and leaves pairs in the same tier unranked. The rule uses the estimates to make these assignments. We use a posterior distribution to assess how often the directions would be wrong and how much the report would cost if withholding also carries a penalty.

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three tiers. Three groups of 10 state 300 of 435 pairs, a share of .690. Under the teaching posterior they expect 51.86 wrong directions, .173 per stated direction, and risk .1813 at τ .20. The marks identify all stated pairs with error above τ, including comparisons across several boundaries.
Ten tiers, marks on. Disclosure rises to 405 pairs (.931), but expected wrong directions rise to 89.40 and E/N to .221. There are 197 marked pairs; the largest stated error is .802. At this τ, the tier rule has risk .2193, compared with .2000 if it withholds every direction. Here τ sets the cost of withholding.
Four tiers. Quantile positions produce sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 and state 337 pairs (.775). The grouped formula counts within-tier withheld pairs. The equal-size closed form disappears because four does not divide thirty.
Two tiers. Groups of 15 state 225 pairs (.517). The triangles in the pair map mark comparisons within a tier. Use the arrow keys to read individual cells.
Thirty tiers. Every pair is stated. The tiers follow the estimates, so their 102.2 expected wrong directions differ from the 94.48 of the posterior-mean ranking in Ranking states many claims. With G set to one, E/N becomes “NA: no disclosure,” while risk is .2000.







The example uses one set of estimates for thirty simulated units and independent normal posteriors based on a prior with mean 0 and SD .15. A change in τ changes the reporting loss and which errors the app marks. The estimates still determine tier membership. If an exact tie spans two tiers, postrank merges those tiers to keep the tied units together.

title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text: The unit with the highest posterior mean can differ from the unit most likely to rank first. A grade report states directions between units. Allocating a place from that report requires a rule for choosing among units in the same grade. Classification at a threshold requires costs for false positives and false negatives.

title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three units, reporting objective. The report has risk .1833. Filling a place from its highest grade selects a unit with expected value 4.000 and top-set overlap .700. The figure gives each quantity its own scale.
Three units, mean-value order. Selecting A instead gives value 6.000 but top-set overlap .300; the strict report’s risk is .4667. The top-set order in the table prefers B. Choosing a first recipient does not require publishing every comparison in a strict order.
Two units, τ .25. The reporting optimum withholds. The added allocation lottery still fills a place, giving expected value 5.000 and overlap .500. It draws the required number of units from the boundary grade.
False-negative cost 3. The threshold rule declares 2 positive, with cost .700. The convention “positive through the highest grade” declares only B positive and costs .900. Neither τ nor the place budget sets the probability cutoff for this decision. Under Threshold 4, being exactly at the substantive threshold does not count as above it. The threshold rule declares 0 positive, at cost .300. The grade cutoff permits both none-positive and all-positive decisions: those actions remain distinct even if a canonical grade representation would lose the distinction.
Equal reporting risk, different classifications. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2, in A/B/C order, both have risk .2000. With the same added grade cutoff, they declare 3 and 2 positive, at costs 1.700 and 1.300. Equal reporting risk does not make the added actions equivalent.
League, five places. Mean-score selection gives value .558 and estimated overlap 2.733. The top-set order gives estimated overlap 2.825. These membership probabilities use the displayed posterior draws; their ordering and overlap evaluation use the same draws.







In these examples, value is the target value of a selected unit. We calculate outcomes exactly for the finite laws. For the league, we calculate the normal means and threshold probabilities analytically and estimate top-set membership and overlap from draws. The league’s reporting optimum is over contiguous cuts of the posterior-mean order under a grade cap. The strict comparison reports do not belong to that family.



Standalone: one-place, for example ?mode=threshold&falseNegativeCost=3.
Related applications: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order, The decision for an isolated pair.

title: Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings
text: A grade report built from an existing ranking inherits that ranking’s order. Quantile tiers also fix the boundaries by group size. Optimal cuts allow those boundaries to vary while keeping the order fixed. For eight units, we can also enumerate the feasible reports and compare both methods with the unrestricted minimum under the same posterior and withholding cost. For the larger examples, we compare cuts of a fixed order. Reports, orders and scopes lists the reports searched and the resulting disclosure counts.

title: Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight units: optimal cuts. Both orders’ cuts state 17 pairs at risk .1455, matching the best of 6,051 reports with at most three grades. Fixed tiers state 21 pairs at risk .1612. This equality between cuts and the joint optimum is a property of these units.
League: fixed tiers. The tiers state 300 pairs at risk .1731. Optimizing their boundaries states 251 at risk .1581. Every rule uses the same posterior and price, but these reports disclose different amounts.
Thirty sites: rank cuts. The cuts state 303 pairs at risk .1603, after searching 4,090 contiguous reports. The orders table shows that the two orders need not coincide for their chosen cuts to agree.
Eight units: all reports. The benchmark expands to 545,835 reports. The reported family determines the scope of the gap for each rule and grade cap.







When the quantile boundaries are among the allowed cuts of an order, the minimum over those cuts cannot have higher risk than the quantile report. Searching other orders may yield a lower minimum within the grade cap. The comparison also depends on the objective. A cut that minimizes directional error can differ from one that minimizes error on a composite score. We do not estimate the gap to the joint optimum for the larger examples.









TipIn postrank





w <- c(poverty = 1, frl = 0, snap = 0); s <- postrank_settings(weights = w, tau = .25, G_max = 4L)
pm <- postrank_cuts(pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"], pr_example_gaussian, s, direction = "descending", method = "posterior_mean")
c(risk = pm$risk)



Standalone: posterior-tiers, for example ?preset=league8-cuts.
Related applications: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order, Restrictions on the report family.

title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text: There are two ways to compare reports that disclose different numbers of pairs. At a common withholding cost, risk includes both expected wrong directions and the cost of the pairs left unranked. At a common number of stated pairs, we compare expected wrong counts directly. We apply both comparisons to the same rules under one posterior. In the thirty-unit example, the comparison family consists of contiguous cuts of one order.

title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same τ, .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with risk .1612, while the best report states 17 with risk .1455. The solid and dashed lines have the same slope. The lower line has lower risk at this τ.
Same N, eight units. The tiers’ gap is .1634 at N 21. The diamond is a frontier mixture, while the square marks the best single report at that N. The rank strip and table compare risk and gap side by side.
Thirty units, one order. The capped family has 436 reports. Posterior-mean tiers state 300 pairs with E 48.31. The boundary gives the lowest expected wrong count available among cuts of this order.
Thirty units, same τ. Without the cap, the family contains 536,870,912 contiguous cuts of the posterior-mean order. There is no enumerated cloud here. Both comparison modes use the same units.
Flags outside the order. The flag report is outside this family: it still has an evaluated risk, but no matched-disclosure benchmark in this order family. The hollow mark records this restriction.
All-withheld. N is 0 and the risk at τ .20 is .2000. Its fraction of stated pairs that are wrong is undefined.







We evaluate the rules under the same normal posterior. The flags use the mean of all thirty estimates as their reference. For thirty units, the boundary comes from the hull of contiguous cuts in the given order. The withholding cost determines the loss, and the report family determines which benchmarks are available. An allocation or classification decision would require its own objective.









NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))



Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=thirty&theme=dark.
Related applications: Comparison at matched disclosure · The error–disclosure frontier.

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text: A report with three balanced tiers states more pairwise directions than a report with two small tiers and one large tier. In both reports, units in different tiers are ranked and units in the same tier are left unranked. The number of pairs in each category follows from the tier sizes. The distribution counts how many ordered size patterns yield each disclosure count. It holds the number of units and tiers fixed and gives each valid size pattern equal weight.

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text:
Numerical illustrations

Balanced thirty. Sizes 10, 10, 10 state 300 of 435 pairs, a share of .690. Each withheld triangle contributes its within-tier count to the grouped formula. Balanced sizes reach the maximum for this number of tiers.
Two tiny tiers. Sizes 1, 1, 28 state only 57 pairs, although they use the same number of tiers. The balanced reference still states 300. Moving the smallest tiers to another position gives the same disclosure but another ordered size pattern.
Four tiers. Sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 state 337 pairs (.775). These tiers reach the largest possible disclosure when four tiers share thirty units.
Balanced twelve. Three groups of four state 48 of 66 pairs. Enter another size vector or move the individual controls to compare groups with the same total.
Unbalanced twelve. Sizes 5, 4, 3 state 47 pairs, below the balanced maximum of 48. A zero size or incorrect total is invalid; the result remains unavailable until the vector is feasible.







The distribution includes every ordered size pattern with at least one unit per tier. A pattern is counted once regardless of how many ways the units could be assigned to it. Quantile rules usually produce nearly balanced sizes, although postrank can merge neighboring tiers to keep equal estimates together. The formula gives the exact number of comparisons for any valid sizes. To assess their accuracy, we would also need the assignments and the probabilities for the pairs they disclose.

Related applications: Fixed quantile tiers, with the full league, pair map and expected wrong directions; The number of ordered grade reports, which counts assignments to ordered grades.

title: Case-report specification and export
text: The tool builds a grade report from the released probabilities for each case. The budget applies to the report on the screen. The reporting view records the outcome, model assumptions, and search used to produce the grades.

title: Case-report specification and export
text:
Numerical illustrations

CDE: three-grade family. The browser enumerates all 523,251 capped reports. The chosen report states 45 pairs. The result applies to the twelve schools in the teaching subset.
KRW: equal weights. The result is labeled “optimal within this order” and states 636 pairs. Changing the weight can change the order and which reports the search considers. The supplied intervals describe race and gender separately.
Alabama: equal weights. The report states 1,249 pairs. Grade 1 indicates favorable historical outcomes, including lower incarceration. The case and its text download give the population and interval level.
CDE: cap two. The family contains 4,095 reports. Compare its best report with the archived report at the same withholding cost.
CDE: mean-order cap four. The computation switches to the posterior-mean order. It is optimal only among cuts of that order. The budget table gives the difference between the allowed and expected error counts.
CDE: all withheld. E/N reads NA: no disclosure. A homogeneous budget passes without stating anything, so a pass alone does not establish useful or error-free disclosure.







The archived status, bound, and gap apply to the archived computation. The current search has its own scope. A shared grade leaves the comparison unstated. The expected error share describes individual comparisons in aggregate, and the probability that every stated comparison is correct requires a joint calculation. A decision to allocate resources would require a further rule. Draft text stays in the open component’s memory.
CDE uses the fitted statewide prior. KRW uses historical contact-gap estimates from Kline, Rose and Walters and their data deposit, under the deposit’s CC-BY-NC terms (no version stated). The experiment describes historical contact gaps. Alabama uses Opportunity Atlas historical outcomes under CC BY 4.0. The case notes and downloads give the source, changes, rights, and conditioning. These details appear on each CSV row. Relations use 1 for row above column, -1 for column above row, 0 for withheld, and NA on the diagonal.









NoteIn postrank





The mean-order cap-four result states 54 pairs, with risk .0368858. With postrank 1.1.0 loaded:
x <- pr_case_cde$input; s <- postrank_settings(weights = c(negative_chronic_absence = 1), tau = .2, G_max = 4)
a <- postrank_cuts(x$summaries$means[, 1], x, s, direction = "descending", rule = "optimal")
a$evaluation[c("N", "E_over_N", "primary_risk")]

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text: Under a jointly normal posterior, the unit with the larger mean is more likely to have the larger true value, whether or not the units are independent. This result depends on the shape of the joint distribution. In the first example, each true value can be 0, 1, or 2. Pairing those values in two ways preserves both marginal distributions but changes π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y) from 1/3 under law 1 to 2/3 under law 2. In the mixture example, a small probability at a large value can make A’s posterior mean larger even though B is more likely to have the larger true value.

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law 1. Each unit’s own posterior, its row or column total, puts 1/3 on each value, and both posterior means are 1.00, yet π_AB = 1/3 and π_BA = 2/3: B is more probably the higher unit. In the figure, w = .20 puts A’s mean at .120, above B’s 0, yet π_AB = .392.
Law 2. Pairing the same marginal values differently raises π_AB to 2/3. The cell frequencies determine the probability of each joint outcome.
Independent. Every pair once: the totals stay at 1/3, but A equals B with probability 1/3, so π_AB = π_BA = 1/3, adding up to 2/3, not one.
Always equal. The same totals, and A always equals B: π_AB = π_BA = 0. Adding a count to a blue cell changes both the margins and π_AB.
w .50. Two equally weighted mixture components: A’s mean, .450, and π_AB = .620 point the same way. Open Why the mean and direction can disagree to see that, among the slider’s settings, the two disagree only for w from .10 to .30.







The two laws are restated from the postrank theory book, ch. 9 (Fig. f09b); the posteriors are set by hand, and every probability is computed in this browser. Tie-freeness, that the two true values are never exactly equal, is an assumption about the joint law: with θ_A = θ_B = Z for one continuous Z, both posteriors are continuous, yet A always equals B. postrank’s postrank_mixture_coefficients() calculates the pair probabilities in each mixture component and averages them using the component weights.



Standalone: embed/beyond-normal.html, for example ?cells=021100010&mixW=.30 or ?preset=law2&theme=dark.
Related applications: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities (1.8) and Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons (1.9) show the jointly normal case.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text: Consecutive Markov chain draws often contain less information about π_AB than the same number of independent draws. The stationary example has two equally probable states, A above B and A below B, so π_AB = 1/2. Increasing the chance of staying in the current state makes consecutive draws more alike and increases the variance of the estimated probability. The transition probabilities give its exact finite-sample variance and the failure rate of the independence-based bound.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Stay .99. Treated as 100 independent draws, the estimate has SD .0500 (its exact SD is .376), and the iid error bound (radius .148) would fail in at most .05 of runs; in these 2,000 chains it fails in .801 (1,602 chains; exact chance .804). A chain that never switches (chance .370) fails by itself.
Stay .99, chain-aware. The exact SD is .376 (variance .1412), compared with .0500 (.002500) for independent draws. This is the variance of 1.77 independent draws. The long-run formula gives 1.01, an approximation for long chains. The bands now span almost all of 0 to 1.
A stuck chain. Chain 7 never switches: its estimate is 0 and its iid MCSE is 0, yet π_AB = 1/2. Of these 2,000 chains, 720 never switch.
Stay .50. Independent draws: correlation 0, the variance of 100 independent draws, and the iid error bound fails in 10 of the 2,000 runs (.005; exact .004), well under .05.
1,000 draws. Ten times as many draws give the variance of 10.6 independent draws, and the iid error bound, now of radius .047, still fails in .777 of these chains (exact .770).
postrank’s chains. In pr_toy_mcmc the pooled share is .172 against the known .2, its MCMC MCSE .0576 against .00835 by the iid formula; R-hat 1.0905 and bulk ESS 42.95 flag the slow mixing. The fixed report’s loss is .248 against 4/15 (.191 to .296 by chain).







The two-state chain is restated from the postrank theory book, ch. 15 (“Finite-sample coefficient error in a stationary two-state chain”); We calculate the exact values from the transition probability and count the outcomes of chains simulated in the browser. In postrank, postrank_iid_bounds() refuses MCMC draws, and postrank_diagnose() reports R-hat, ESS and an MCMC MCSE for them (vignette m6, “Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics”).









TipIn postrank





library(postrank); law <- attr(pr_toy_mcmc, "law")
mc <- postrank_draws(pr_toy_mcmc, regime = "mcmc", chains = 4L, warmup_per_chain = 0L, thin = 1L, declarations = law$declarations)
postrank_diagnose(mc, pairs = data.frame(entity_i = "A", entity_j = "B", criterion_id = "k1"))$summaries$pair_1$diagnostics   # values: rhat 1.090465, ess_bulk 42.95484, mcse_mean 0.05764243 (1.0905, 42.95, .0576)



Standalone: embed/chain-draws.html, for example ?stay=.95&draws=200 or ?preset=aware&theme=dark.
Related applications: From data to posterior decisions (1.7) lists the forms a posterior can take: postrank validates the structure of draws, and its MCMC diagnostics flag problems but do not prove convergence. Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities (1.17) shows the Monte Carlo error of independent draws.

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text: The majority-win count Hᵢ = #{j:Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ ∣ Y) > 1/2} counts the units that i is more likely to exceed. Expected rank uses the full probabilities, R̄ᵢ↓ = 1 + ∑_j≠i Pr(θⱼ > θᵢ ∣ Y). Under independent normal posteriors, ordering the win counts gives the same ranking as ordering the posterior means. The simulated and archived examples show how the rankings can diverge under other distributions. We also compare them with the cards of Kline, Rose and Walters (KRW) at λ = 1, when a correct direction earns as much as an incorrect direction costs.

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law on orders. A beats B and C, each only with probability .51; B’s one win is nearly sure (.99). A has the most wins. B has the best expected rank, 1.52 compared with A’s 1.98.
League. Majority wins give the posterior-mean order: 0 of the 435 pairs differ. The expected-rank order states 6 pairs against the majority; U13 is 8th by it (9.59) and 6th by the other two.
League, prior SD .30. The win count and posterior-mean order still disagree on 0 of the 435 pairs. Expected rank now orders 12 pairs against the majority.
KRW, race. Majority wins form a strict order. Against it the posterior-mean order states 35 of the 4,656 pairs and the expected-rank order 62; KRW’s card at λ = 1 states none against it, so no full ranking expects fewer wrong claims: 1,248, against 1,249 for the posterior-mean order.
KRW, gender. Macy’s beats Jones Lang LaSalle (.5008), which beats Dollar General (.5022), which beats Macy’s (.5014): a cycle, and the three win 45 pairs each. KRW’s card at λ = 1 (96 grades) puts Macy’s and Dollar General in one grade, within KRW’s solver tolerances.







KRW call the grades at λ = 1 Condorcet ranks (Section II.F). Their remark there that the count of wins is equivalent to the posterior mean rank (the expected rank) does not hold in general: on the race gaps, majority wins and the expected rank order 62 pairs differently. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), A Discrimination Report Card, American Economic Review, doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only. Pair probabilities as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW’s code (KRW replication companion) under KRW’s archived pair probabilities (KRW’s cards along λ). Changes noted; no endorsement by the authors is implied.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank); r <- pr_case_krw$alternatives$race; e <- r$e[, , 1]
w <- rowSums(e < t(e), na.rm = TRUE); pm <- postrank_posterior_means(r)[, 1]; er <- postrank_expected_rank(r)
c(mean = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(pm, pm, "<")), rank = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(er, er, ">")))   # 35 62

title: Estimates and sampling error
text: An estimate can change from one sample to the next even when the quantity it measures stays fixed. In this simulation, we add normally distributed sampling error to the same true value on each draw. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the estimates across draws. About two-thirds of the estimates fall within one SE of the true value. The figure separates the latest estimate into its true value and the sampling error that moved it away from that value.

title: Estimates and sampling error
text:
Numerical illustrations

SE .20. Twenty estimates of a unit whose true value is .50: 12 of 20 fall within one SE (the filled dots), against 13.65 expected on average. The ringed latest estimate, .229, is the true value plus noise −.271.
200 draws. With ten times as many draws, the count within one SE moves from 12 of 20 to 132 of 200, against 136.54 expected, while the share expected on average stays .6827.
Seed 2. With a different sample, 18 of 20 estimates for the same unit fall within one SE. The model still predicts an average count of 13.65.
SE .10. Seed 1 again with half the SE: every estimate moves halfway toward the true value and the noise arrow halves to −.136, yet each draw keeps its noise in SEs (−1.36), so the count stays 12 of 20.
SE .05. Halving the SE again gives the same standardized errors: the noise is −.068, and still 12 of 20 fall within one SE. The three SEs are those of the small, medium and large units in Ranking noisy estimates.







We generate sampling errors by multiplying standard normal draws by the SE. Returning to the same seed reproduces the same draws. This is the model of Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III, Assumption 1 (stated before Section III.A), and talk slide 17. Walters’ Mixtape slides (pp. 5–6) set it up the same way, and the postrank theory book, ch. 2, “Teacher growth categories: evidence, precision, and the choice of assessment”, reads estimates together with their standard errors.



Standalone: embed/noisy-estimate.html, for example ?se=.10&draws=50 or ?preset=seed2&theme=dark.
Related applications: Ranking noisy estimates · Normal–normal posterior shrinkage.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text: We compare interval overlap and posterior direction probabilities for all 435 pairs of the thirty simulated units. The intervals come from the model in normal–normal posterior shrinkage. For a selected pair, the figure shows how far the intervals overlap and the probability that the first unit has the larger true value. The table counts the pairs with overlapping intervals and identifies those that still have a direction probability above .90. Changing the interval level or the prior standard deviation changes these counts.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overlap, highest probability. 399 of the 435 pairs have overlapping 90% intervals, and 88 of them still have one direction above .90. The highest is .988, for U13 above U05, whose intervals overlap by .005: no overlapping pair is above .99.
U06 and U20. These intervals do not overlap (.002 lies between them), and U06 is the higher with probability .988, the same to three decimals as the preceding pair, whose intervals overlap.
U04 and U18. A wide overlap, .107, and still U04 is the higher with probability .904: U18’s narrow interval ends at −.105, below U04’s posterior mean, −.014.
95% intervals. Wider intervals overlap more often, in 413 pairs, and 102 of these have one direction above .90. The highest is now .997, for U03 above U15.
Prior SD .05. A narrow prior pulls every posterior mean toward zero: 427 pairs overlap, only 58 of them with one direction above .90.







For two independent normal posteriors, whatever their SDs, the more likely direction has a probability above .950 when their 90% intervals do not overlap. When they overlap, it is at most .990, the value for equal SDs and intervals that just touch (.975 and .997 for 95% intervals). Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C) draw a credible interval beside each name, but they grade the names from pairwise posterior probabilities.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text: A grade report requires a posterior distribution and a rule for deciding which comparisons to state. The analyst chooses a model and prior and fits them to the observed data Y to obtain Pr(θ ∣ Y). postrank uses the resulting posterior to select a grade report. The four boxes trace these steps for two units and identify which choices the analyst makes. The table beneath the boxes lists which calculations are available for each representation of the posterior.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Box 1 (Data). Y holds the estimates and their SEs: .25 (SE .10) for A and .05 (SE .20) for B. postrank never reads Y itself, only a posterior computed from it.
Box 2 (Model). The prior SD, .15, is the analyst’s choice, set by hand here. With each SE it sets how much of its estimate each posterior mean keeps: .692 for A, .360 for the noisier B.
Box 3 (Posterior). The posterior is the input to postrank. The posterior means are .173 and .018, and π = .856 is the probability that A is truly higher. B more precise (SE .10, as for A): B keeps .692 too, its mean is .035, and π rises to .880.
Box 4 (Decision). The postrank step: stating A above B is wrong with probability .144, less than τ = .20, so postrank states it, {A} > {B}, the best of all 3 reports. At τ .10 withholding costs less than .144, so postrank withholds the pair: {A, B}.
Prior SD .05. With a narrower prior, A’s posterior mean falls to .050 and π to .762. Stating A above B would now be wrong with probability .238, so postrank withholds the pair: {A, B}. The prior changes the report through its effect on the posterior probability.







Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III.A–B, set out the empirical Bayes posteriors behind their firm grades (KRW call them beliefs). In their talk, slides 34 and 37 show the model for first names, not for the firms; slides 43 to 52 set out the empirical Bayes model for the firms. Walters’ Mixtape slides on empirical Bayes (p. 13) set out the same recipe. The two units here are set by hand, and the browser computes their posterior; postrank fits no model.

title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text: A smaller prior standard deviation pulls posterior means closer to the prior mean in the normal–normal model. Analysts may choose the prior standard deviation or estimate it from the data by empirical Bayes. We vary it from .01 to 1 for the same simulated league used in normal–normal posterior shrinkage. With the prior centered on the average true value, posterior means have the smallest average squared error when the prior spread is close to the spread of the true values. The prior standard deviation also changes the posterior probability of each direction. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.

title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Near the true spread. At prior SD .15 both distance curves are at their lowest point among the slider’s settings: .0096 in this draw (the estimates: .0163) and .0075 over many draws. A finer search puts the closed form’s lowest point at about .146, next to the true spread, .149.
Much too narrow. At .02 the posterior means end farther from the true values than the estimates: .0197 against .0163 in this draw, .0191 against .0175 over many draws. In this draw the posterior puts one direction above .90 in only 6 of the 435 pairs.
Too narrow. At .05 the expected pairs against the true order are 87.45, against 88.12 for the estimates and 80.66 at their fewest; in this draw 17 units end farther than their estimates were.
Too wide. At .45 the expected distance is .0133, as at .05, yet in this draw the posterior puts one direction above .90 in 159 pairs instead of 66. These are the posterior’s own probabilities; whether such directions are right under the true values is checked in Reported error and reference-law evaluation. In this draw 13 units end farther, as at every prior SD from about .23 on.
Another draw. With seed 20261031 this draw’s distance is lowest at .12 (.0092); over many draws it stays lowest at .15 (.0075).







The curve labeled “Over many draws” gives the expected error across samples with the true values fixed. We compute this expectation in closed form. The postrank theory book (ch. 18) calls this a fixed-parameter experiment. postrank fits no model and reads the posterior it is given (ch. 18, “Hyperparameters, precision and represented uncertainty”). The best report at each prior SD and the error share it claims are shown in Reported error and reference-law evaluation. The normal–normal shrinkage follows Walters’ Mixtape slides (p. 27).

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text: For two units A and B, π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y) is the posterior probability that A’s true value exceeds B’s. The probability is the area above zero under the posterior distribution of A − B. With independent normal posteriors, the variance of this difference equals the sum of the two marginal variances. The figure puts both marginals and their difference on the same scales so the reader can see how the two uncertainties enter the comparison.

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .20. The two posteriors overlap substantially, while π_AB = .760. The SD of the difference is .283. A’s mean is .707 of these SDs above B’s.
Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .60 (B much less precise). The same gap, but the difference widens to SD .632, so A’s mean is only .316 SDs of it above B’s, and π_AB falls to .624, closer to one half.
Means .20 and .20, SDs .20 and .40. With equal means each direction has probability .500, for either choice of marginal SDs; the difference keeps mean 0 and only spreads out (SD .447).
Means 1.20 and .95, SDs .20 and .20 (tutorial sites A and B). Sites A and B of the six fictional sites in postrank’s tutorial data: π_AB = .812. The package stores one minus this number, the chance that stating A above B would be wrong.







The example specifies two independent normal posteriors. Under this model, the unit with the larger posterior mean is more likely to have the larger true value for any positive SDs. Also, π_BA = 1 − π_AB, because the two true values have probability zero of being equal. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.E, Example 1, and slide 27 of their talk, use the special case of this formula with both SDs equal to 1.

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text: The largest estimates in a ranking tend to overstate their units’ true values because units with positive sampling errors are more likely to rank near the top. The reverse holds at the bottom. In a simulation of thirty units, we compare estimates and posterior means with the true values of units selected by their estimates. A normal prior centered on the average true value, with a standard deviation close to the true spread, reduces the average upward bias of the highest estimates. The posterior means differ from the true values by −.007 on average in this example.

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text:
Numerical illustrations

Top 3. Over the 2,000 replays, estimate minus true value averages .160 for the top 3 by estimate; for their posterior means at prior SD .15, near the true values’ spread of .149, it averages −.007. Replay 1 is the draw that 1.3 and 1.5 show first: .071 and −.031.
Replay 9. In this sample, the differences from the true values average −.043 for the top 3 estimates and −.117 for their posterior means. The average bias across samples allows for individual samples like this one.
Top 1. Over the replays, the largest estimate overshoots most: .220 above its unit’s true value on average, against .081 for the top 10 (set k to 10). Its posterior mean averages −.024.
Bottom 3. The lower-tail comparison has the opposite sign: on average over the replays the bottom 3 sit below their true values, −.150, and their posterior means have average difference −.013.
Prior SD .05. A prior narrower than the true spread induces excessive shrinkage: on average over the replays the top 3’s posterior means end at −.131, below their true values (at prior SD .10, −.063).







Walters (2024, Handbook of Labor Economics, section 3.5) points to the upward bias of the largest estimate that the ranking step creates. Andrews, Kitagawa and McCloskey (2024, “Inference on Winners”) give inference on the top unit’s value that accounts for it. The posterior here comes from one normal prior set by hand for teaching; postrank does not fit it. The reporting procedure takes the resulting posterior as its input. In an application, the analyst cannot check these differences directly because the true values are unknown.
